1|.. py:currentmodule:: jinja2
2|.. highlight:: html+jinja
3|
4|Template Designer Documentation
5|===============================
6|
7|This document describes the syntax and semantics of the template engine and
8|will be most useful as reference to those creating Jinja templates.  As the
9|template engine is very flexible, the configuration from the application can
10|be slightly different from the code presented here in terms of delimiters and
11|behavior of undefined values.
12|
13|
14|Synopsis
15|--------
16|
17|A Jinja template is simply a text file. Jinja can generate any text-based
18|format (HTML, XML, CSV, LaTeX, etc.).  A Jinja template doesn't need to have a
19|specific extension: ``.html``, ``.xml``, or any other extension is just fine.
20|
21|A template contains **variables** and/or **expressions**, which get replaced
22|with values when a template is *rendered*; and **tags**, which control the
23|logic of the template.  The template syntax is heavily inspired by Django and
24|Python.
25|
26|Below is a minimal template that illustrates a few basics using the default
27|Jinja configuration.  We will cover the details later in this document::
28|
29|    <!DOCTYPE html>
30|    <html lang="en">
31|    <head>
32|        <title>My Webpage</title>
33|    </head>
34|    <body>
35|        <ul id="navigation">
36|        {% for item in navigation %}
37|            <li><a href="{{ item.href }}">{{ item.caption }}</a></li>
38|        {% endfor %}
39|        </ul>
40|
41|        <h1>My Webpage</h1>
42|        {{ a_variable }}
43|
44|        {# a comment #}
45|    </body>
46|    </html>
47|
48|The following example shows the default configuration settings.  An application
49|developer can change the syntax configuration from ``{% foo %}`` to ``<% foo
50|%>``, or something similar.
51|
52|There are a few kinds of delimiters. The default Jinja delimiters are
53|configured as follows:
54|
55|* ``{% ... %}`` for :ref:`Statements <list-of-control-structures>`
56|* ``{{ ... }}`` for :ref:`Expressions` to print to the template output
57|* ``{# ... #}`` for :ref:`Comments` not included in the template output
58|
59|:ref:`Line Statements and Comments <line-statements>` are also possible,
60|though they don't have default prefix characters. To use them, set
61|``line_statement_prefix`` and ``line_comment_prefix`` when creating the
62|:class:`~jinja2.Environment`.
63|
64|
65|Template File Extension
66|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
67|
68|As stated above, any file can be loaded as a template, regardless of
69|file extension. Adding a ``.jinja`` extension, like ``user.html.jinja``
70|may make it easier for some IDEs or editor plugins, but is not required.
71|Autoescaping, introduced later, can be applied based on file extension,
72|so you'll need to take the extra suffix into account in that case.
73|
74|Another good heuristic for identifying templates is that they are in a
75|``templates`` folder, regardless of extension. This is a common layout
76|for projects.
77|
78|
79|.. _variables:
80|
81|Variables
82|---------
83|
84|Template variables are defined by the context dictionary passed to the
85|template.
86|
87|You can mess around with the variables in templates provided they are passed in
88|by the application.  Variables may have attributes or elements on them you can
89|access too.  What attributes a variable has depends heavily on the application
90|providing that variable.
91|
92|You can use a dot (``.``) to access attributes of a variable in addition
93|to the standard Python ``__getitem__`` "subscript" syntax (``[]``).
94|
95|The following lines do the same thing::
96|
97|    {{ foo.bar }}
98|    {{ foo['bar'] }}
99|
100|It's important to know that the outer double-curly braces are *not* part of the
101|variable, but the print statement.  If you access variables inside tags don't
102|put the braces around them.
103|
104|If a variable or attribute does not exist, you will get back an undefined
105|value.  What you can do with that kind of value depends on the application
106|configuration: the default behavior is to evaluate to an empty string if
107|printed or iterated over, and to fail for every other operation.
108|
109|.. _notes-on-subscriptions:
110|
111|.. admonition:: Implementation
112|
113|    For the sake of convenience, ``foo.bar`` in Jinja does the following
114|    things on the Python layer:
115|
116|    -   check for an attribute called `bar` on `foo`
117|        (``getattr(foo, 'bar')``)
118|    -   if there is not, check for an item ``'bar'`` in `foo`
119|        (``foo.__getitem__('bar')``)
120|    -   if there is not, return an undefined object.
121|
122|    ``foo['bar']`` works mostly the same with a small difference in sequence:
123|
124|    -   check for an item ``'bar'`` in `foo`.
125|        (``foo.__getitem__('bar')``)
126|    -   if there is not, check for an attribute called `bar` on `foo`.
127|        (``getattr(foo, 'bar')``)
128|    -   if there is not, return an undefined object.
129|
130|    This is important if an object has an item and attribute with the same
131|    name.  Additionally, the :func:`attr` filter only looks up attributes.
132|
133|.. _filters:
134|
135|Filters
136|-------
137|
138|Variables can be modified by **filters**.  Filters are separated from the
139|variable by a pipe symbol (``|``) and may have optional arguments in
140|parentheses.  Multiple filters can be chained.  The output of one filter is
141|applied to the next.
142|
143|For example, ``{{ name|striptags|title }}`` will remove all HTML Tags from
144|variable `name` and title-case the output (``title(striptags(name))``).
145|
146|Filters that accept arguments have parentheses around the arguments, just like
147|a function call.  For example: ``{{ listx|join(', ') }}`` will join a list with
148|commas (``str.join(', ', listx)``).
149|
150|The :ref:`builtin-filters` below describes all the builtin filters.
151|
152|.. _tests:
153|
154|Tests
155|-----
156|
157|Beside filters, there are also so-called "tests" available.  Tests can be used
158|to test a variable against a common expression.  To test a variable or
159|expression, you add `is` plus the name of the test after the variable.  For
160|example, to find out if a variable is defined, you can do ``name is defined``,
161|which will then return true or false depending on whether `name` is defined
162|in the current template context.
163|
164|Tests can accept arguments, too.  If the test only takes one argument, you can
165|leave out the parentheses.  For example, the following two
166|expressions do the same thing::
167|
168|    {% if loop.index is divisibleby 3 %}
169|    {% if loop.index is divisibleby(3) %}
170|
171|The :ref:`builtin-tests` below describes all the builtin tests.
172|
173|
174|.. _comments:
175|
176|Comments
177|--------
178|
179|To comment-out part of a line in a template, use the comment syntax which is
180|by default set to ``{# ... #}``.  This is useful to comment out parts of the
181|template for debugging or to add information for other template designers or
182|yourself::
183|
184|    {# note: commented-out template because we no longer use this
185|        {% for user in users %}
186|            ...
187|        {% endfor %}
188|    #}
189|
190|
191|Whitespace Control
192|------------------
193|
194|In the default configuration:
195|
196|* a single trailing newline is stripped if present
197|* other whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines etc.) is returned unchanged
198|
199|If an application configures Jinja to `trim_blocks`, the first newline after a
200|template tag is removed automatically (like in PHP). The `lstrip_blocks`
201|option can also be set to strip tabs and spaces from the beginning of a
202|line to the start of a block. (Nothing will be stripped if there are
203|other characters before the start of the block.)
204|
205|With both ``trim_blocks`` and ``lstrip_blocks`` disabled (the default), block
206|tags on their own lines will be removed, but a blank line will remain and the
207|spaces in the content will be preserved. For example, this template:
208|
209|.. code-block:: jinja
210|
211|    <div>
212|        {% if True %}
213|            yay
214|        {% endif %}
215|    </div>
216|
217|With both ``trim_blocks`` and ``lstrip_blocks`` disabled, the template is
218|rendered with blank lines inside the div:
219|
220|.. code-block:: text
221|
222|    <div>
223|
224|            yay
225|
226|    </div>
227|
228|With both ``trim_blocks`` and ``lstrip_blocks`` enabled, the template block
229|lines are completely removed:
230|
231|.. code-block:: text
232|
233|    <div>
234|            yay
235|    </div>
236|
237|You can manually disable the `lstrip_blocks` behavior by putting a
238|plus sign (``+``) at the start of a block::
239|
240|    <div>
241|            {%+ if something %}yay{% endif %}
242|    </div>
243|
244|Similarly, you can manually disable the ``trim_blocks`` behavior by
245|putting a plus sign (``+``) at the end of a block::
246|
247|    <div>
248|        {% if something +%}
249|            yay
250|        {% endif %}
251|    </div>
252|
253|You can also strip whitespace in templates by hand.  If you add a minus
254|sign (``-``) to the start or end of a block (e.g. a :ref:`for-loop` tag), a
255|comment, or a variable expression, the whitespaces before or after
256|that block will be removed::
257|
258|    {% for item in seq -%}
259|        {{ item }}
260|    {%- endfor %}
261|
262|This will yield all elements without whitespace between them.  If `seq` was
263|a list of numbers from ``1`` to ``9``, the output would be ``123456789``.
264|
265|If :ref:`line-statements` are enabled, they strip leading whitespace
266|automatically up to the beginning of the line.
267|
268|By default, Jinja also removes trailing newlines.  To keep single
269|trailing newlines, configure Jinja to `keep_trailing_newline`.
270|
271|.. admonition:: Note
272|
273|    You must not add whitespace between the tag and the minus sign.
274|
275|    **valid**::
276|
277|        {%- if foo -%}...{% endif %}
278|
279|    **invalid**::
280|
281|        {% - if foo - %}...{% endif %}
282|
283|
284|Escaping
285|--------
286|
287|It is sometimes desirable -- even necessary -- to have Jinja ignore parts
288|it would otherwise handle as variables or blocks.  For example, if, with
289|the default syntax, you want to use ``{{`` as a raw string in a template and
290|not start a variable, you have to use a trick.
291|
292|The easiest way to output a literal variable delimiter (``{{``) is by using a
293|variable expression::
294|
295|    {{ '{{' }}
296|
297|For bigger sections, it makes sense to mark a block `raw`.  For example, to
298|include example Jinja syntax in a template, you can use this snippet::
299|
300|    {% raw %}
301|        <ul>
302|        {% for item in seq %}
303|            <li>{{ item }}</li>
304|        {% endfor %}
305|        </ul>
306|    {% endraw %}
307|
308|.. admonition:: Note
309|
310|    Minus sign at the end of ``{% raw -%}`` tag cleans all the spaces and newlines
311|    preceding the first character of your raw data.
312|
313|
314|.. _line-statements:
315|
316|Line Statements
317|---------------
318|
319|If line statements are enabled by the application, it's possible to mark a
320|line as a statement.  For example, if the line statement prefix is configured
321|to ``#``, the following two examples are equivalent::
322|
323|    <ul>
324|    # for item in seq
325|        <li>{{ item }}</li>
326|    # endfor
327|    </ul>
328|
329|    <ul>
330|    {% for item in seq %}
331|        <li>{{ item }}</li>
332|    {% endfor %}
333|    </ul>
334|
335|The line statement prefix can appear anywhere on the line as long as no text
336|precedes it.  For better readability, statements that start a block (such as
337|`for`, `if`, `elif` etc.) may end with a colon::
338|
339|    # for item in seq:
340|        ...
341|    # endfor
342|
343|
344|.. admonition:: Note
345|
346|    Line statements can span multiple lines if there are open parentheses,
347|    braces or brackets::
348|
349|        <ul>
350|        # for href, caption in [('index.html', 'Index'),
351|                                ('about.html', 'About')]:
352|            <li><a href="{{ href }}">{{ caption }}</a></li>
353|        # endfor
354|        </ul>
355|
356|Since Jinja 2.2, line-based comments are available as well.  For example, if
357|the line-comment prefix is configured to be ``##``, everything from ``##`` to
358|the end of the line is ignored (excluding the newline sign)::
359|
360|    # for item in seq:
361|        <li>{{ item }}</li>     ## this comment is ignored
362|    # endfor
363|
364|
365|.. _template-inheritance:
366|
367|Template Inheritance
368|--------------------
369|
370|The most powerful part of Jinja is template inheritance. Template inheritance
371|allows you to build a base "skeleton" template that contains all the common
372|elements of your site and defines **blocks** that child templates can override.
373|
374|Sounds complicated but is very basic. It's easiest to understand it by starting
375|with an example.
376|
377|
378|Base Template
379|~~~~~~~~~~~~~
380|
381|This template, which we'll call ``base.html``, defines a simple HTML skeleton
382|document that you might use for a simple two-column page. It's the job of
383|"child" templates to fill the empty blocks with content::
384|
385|    <!DOCTYPE html>
386|    <html lang="en">
387|    <head>
388|        {% block head %}
389|        <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" />
390|        <title>{% block title %}{% endblock %} - My Webpage</title>
391|        {% endblock %}
392|    </head>
393|    <body>
394|        <div id="content">{% block content %}{% endblock %}</div>
395|        <div id="footer">
396|            {% block footer %}
397|            © Copyright 2008 by <a href="http://domain.invalid/">you</a>.
398|            {% endblock %}
399|        </div>
400|    </body>
401|    </html>
402|
403|In this example, the ``{% block %}`` tags define four blocks that child templates
404|can fill in. All the `block` tag does is tell the template engine that a
405|child template may override those placeholders in the template.
406|
407|``block`` tags can be inside other blocks such as ``if``, but they will
408|always be executed regardless of if the ``if`` block is actually
409|rendered.
410|
411|Child Template
412|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
413|
414|A child template might look like this::
415|
416|    {% extends "base.html" %}
417|    {% block title %}Index{% endblock %}
418|    {% block head %}
419|        {{ super() }}
420|        <style type="text/css">
421|            .important { color: #336699; }
422|        </style>
423|    {% endblock %}
424|    {% block content %}
425|        <h1>Index</h1>
426|        <p class="important">
427|          Welcome to my awesome homepage.
428|        </p>
429|    {% endblock %}
430|
431|The ``{% extends %}`` tag is the key here. It tells the template engine that
432|this template "extends" another template.  When the template system evaluates
433|this template, it first locates the parent.  The extends tag should be the
434|first tag in the template.  Everything before it is printed out normally and
435|may cause confusion.  For details about this behavior and how to take
436|advantage of it, see :ref:`null-default-fallback`. Also a block will always be
437|filled in regardless of whether the surrounding condition is evaluated to be true
438|or false.
439|
440|The filename of the template depends on the template loader.  For example, the
441|:class:`FileSystemLoader` allows you to access other templates by giving the
442|filename.  You can access templates in subdirectories with a slash::
443|
444|    {% extends "layout/default.html" %}
445|
446|But this behavior can depend on the application embedding Jinja.  Note that
447|since the child template doesn't define the ``footer`` block, the value from
448|the parent template is used instead.
449|
450|You can't define multiple ``{% block %}`` tags with the same name in the
451|same template.  This limitation exists because a block tag works in "both"
452|directions.  That is, a block tag doesn't just provide a placeholder to fill
453|- it also defines the content that fills the placeholder in the *parent*.
454|If there were two similarly-named ``{% block %}`` tags in a template,
455|that template's parent wouldn't know which one of the blocks' content to use.
456|
457|If you want to print a block multiple times, you can, however, use the special
458|`self` variable and call the block with that name::
459|
460|    <title>{% block title %}{% endblock %}</title>
461|    <h1>{{ self.title() }}</h1>
462|    {% block body %}{% endblock %}
463|
464|
465|Super Blocks
466|~~~~~~~~~~~~
467|
468|It's possible to render the contents of the parent block by calling ``super()``.
469|This gives back the results of the parent block::
470|
471|    {% block sidebar %}
472|        <h3>Table Of Contents</h3>
473|        ...
474|        {{ super() }}
475|    {% endblock %}
476|
477|
478|Nesting extends
479|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
480|
481|In the case of multiple levels of ``{% extends %}``,
482|``super`` references may be chained (as in ``super.super()``)
483|to skip levels in the inheritance tree.
484|
485|For example::
486|
487|    # parent.tmpl
488|    body: {% block body %}Hi from parent.{% endblock %}
489|
490|    # child.tmpl
491|    {% extends "parent.tmpl" %}
492|    {% block body %}Hi from child. {{ super() }}{% endblock %}
493|
494|    # grandchild1.tmpl
495|    {% extends "child.tmpl" %}
496|    {% block body %}Hi from grandchild1.{% endblock %}
497|
498|    # grandchild2.tmpl
499|    {% extends "child.tmpl" %}
500|    {% block body %}Hi from grandchild2. {{ super.super() }} {% endblock %}
501|
502|
503|Rendering ``child.tmpl`` will give
504|``body: Hi from child. Hi from parent.``
505|
506|Rendering ``grandchild1.tmpl`` will give
507|``body: Hi from grandchild1.``
508|
509|Rendering ``grandchild2.tmpl`` will give
510|``body: Hi from grandchild2. Hi from parent.``
511|
512|
513|Named Block End-Tags
514|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
515|
516|Jinja allows you to put the name of the block after the end tag for better
517|readability::
518|
519|    {% block sidebar %}
520|        {% block inner_sidebar %}
521|            ...
522|        {% endblock inner_sidebar %}
523|    {% endblock sidebar %}
524|
525|However, the name after the `endblock` word must match the block name.
526|
527|
528|Block Nesting and Scope
529|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
530|
531|Blocks can be nested for more complex layouts. By default, a block may not
532|access variables from outside the block (outer scopes)::
533|
534|    {% for item in seq %}
535|        <li>{% block loop_item %}{{ item }}{% endblock %}</li>
536|    {% endfor %}
537|
538|This example would output empty ``<li>`` items because `item` is unavailable
539|inside the block.  The reason for this is that if the block is replaced by
540|a child template, a variable would appear that was not defined in the block or
541|passed to the context.
542|
543|Starting with Jinja 2.2, you can explicitly specify that variables are
544|available in a block by setting the block to "scoped" by adding the `scoped`
545|modifier to a block declaration::
546|
547|    {% for item in seq %}
548|        <li>{% block loop_item scoped %}{{ item }}{% endblock %}</li>
549|    {% endfor %}
550|
551|When overriding a block, the `scoped` modifier does not have to be provided.
552|
553|
554|Required Blocks
555|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
556|
557|Blocks can be marked as ``required``. They must be overridden at some
558|point, but not necessarily by the direct child template. Required blocks
559|may only contain space and comments, and they cannot be rendered
560|directly.
561|
562|.. code-block:: jinja
563|    :caption: ``page.txt``
564|
565|    {% block body required %}{% endblock %}
566|
567|.. code-block:: jinja
568|    :caption: ``issue.txt``
569|
570|    {% extends "page.txt" %}
571|
572|.. code-block:: jinja
573|    :caption: ``bug_report.txt``
574|
575|    {% extends "issue.txt" %}
576|    {% block body %}Provide steps to demonstrate the bug.{% endblock %}
577|
578|Rendering ``page.txt`` or ``issue.txt`` will raise
579|``TemplateRuntimeError`` because they don't override the ``body`` block.
580|Rendering ``bug_report.txt`` will succeed because it does override the
581|block.
582|
583|When combined with ``scoped``, the ``required`` modifier must be placed
584|*after* the scoped modifier. Here are some valid examples:
585|
586|.. code-block:: jinja
587|
588|    {% block body scoped %}{% endblock %}
589|    {% block body required %}{% endblock %}
590|    {% block body scoped required %}{% endblock %}
591|
592|
593|Template Objects
594|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
595|
596|``extends``, ``include``, and ``import`` can take a template object
597|instead of the name of a template to load. This could be useful in some
598|advanced situations, since you can use Python code to load a template
599|first and pass it in to ``render``.
600|
601|.. code-block:: python
602|
603|    if debug_mode:
604|        layout = env.get_template("debug_layout.html")
605|    else:
606|        layout = env.get_template("layout.html")
607|
608|    user_detail = env.get_template("user/detail.html")
609|    return user_detail.render(layout=layout)
610|
611|.. code-block:: jinja
612|
613|    {% extends layout %}
614|
615|Note how ``extends`` is passed the variable with the template object
616|that was passed to ``render``, instead of a string.
617|
618|
619|HTML Escaping
620|-------------
621|
622|When generating HTML from templates, there's always a risk that a variable will
623|include characters that affect the resulting HTML. There are two approaches:
624|
625|a. manually escaping each variable; or
626|b. automatically escaping everything by default.
627|
628|Jinja supports both. What is used depends on the application configuration.
629|The default configuration is no automatic escaping; for various reasons:
630|
631|-   Escaping everything except for safe values will also mean that Jinja is
632|    escaping variables known to not include HTML (e.g. numbers, booleans)
633|    which can be a huge performance hit.
634|
635|-   The information about the safety of a variable is very fragile.  It could
636|    happen that by coercing safe and unsafe values, the return value is
637|    double-escaped HTML.
638|
639|Working with Manual Escaping
640|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
641|
642|If manual escaping is enabled, it's **your** responsibility to escape
643|variables if needed.  What to escape?  If you have a variable that *may*
644|include any of the following chars (``>``, ``<``, ``&``, or ``"``) you
645|**SHOULD** escape it unless the variable contains well-formed and trusted
646|HTML.  Escaping works by piping the variable through the ``|e`` filter::
647|
648|    {{ user.username|e }}
649|
650|Working with Automatic Escaping
651|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
652|
653|When automatic escaping is enabled, everything is escaped by default except
654|for values explicitly marked as safe.  Variables and expressions
655|can be marked as safe either in:
656|
657|a.  The context dictionary by the application with
658|    :class:`markupsafe.Markup`
659|b.  The template, with the ``|safe`` filter.
660|
661|If a string that you marked safe is passed through other Python code
662|that doesn't understand that mark, it may get lost. Be aware of when
663|your data is marked safe and how it is processed before arriving at the
664|template.
665|
666|If a value has been escaped but is not marked safe, auto-escaping will
667|still take place and result in double-escaped characters. If you know
668|you have data that is already safe but not marked, be sure to wrap it in
669|``Markup`` or use the ``|safe`` filter.
670|
671|Jinja functions (macros, `super`, `self.BLOCKNAME`) always return template
672|data that is marked as safe.
673|
674|String literals in templates with automatic escaping are considered
675|unsafe because native Python strings are not safe.
676|
677|.. _list-of-control-structures:
678|
679|List of Control Structures
680|--------------------------
681|
682|A control structure refers to all those things that control the flow of a
683|program - conditionals (i.e. if/elif/else), for-loops, as well as things like
684|macros and blocks.  With the default syntax, control structures appear inside
685|``{% ... %}`` blocks.
686|
687|.. _for-loop:
688|
689|For
690|~~~
691|
692|Loop over each item in a sequence.  For example, to display a list of users
693|provided in a variable called `users`::
694|
695|    <h1>Members</h1>
696|    <ul>
697|    {% for user in users %}
698|      <li>{{ user.username|e }}</li>
699|    {% endfor %}
700|    </ul>
701|
702|As variables in templates retain their object properties, it is possible to
703|iterate over containers like `dict`::
704|
705|    <dl>
706|    {% for key, value in my_dict.items() %}
707|        <dt>{{ key|e }}</dt>
708|        <dd>{{ value|e }}</dd>
709|    {% endfor %}
710|    </dl>
711|
712|Python dicts may not be in the order you want to display them in. If
713|order matters, use the ``|dictsort`` filter.
714|
715|.. code-block:: jinja
716|
717|    <dl>
718|    {% for key, value in my_dict | dictsort %}
719|        <dt>{{ key|e }}</dt>
720|        <dd>{{ value|e }}</dd>
721|    {% endfor %}
722|    </dl>
723|
724|Inside of a for-loop block, you can access some special variables:
725|
726|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
727|| Variable              | Description                                       |
728|+=======================+===================================================+
729|| `loop.index`          | The current iteration of the loop. (1 indexed)    |
730|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
731|| `loop.index0`         | The current iteration of the loop. (0 indexed)    |
732|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
733|| `loop.revindex`       | The number of iterations from the end of the loop |
734||                       | (1 indexed)                                       |
735|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
736|| `loop.revindex0`      | The number of iterations from the end of the loop |
737||                       | (0 indexed)                                       |
738|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
739|| `loop.first`          | True if first iteration.                          |
740|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
741|| `loop.last`           | True if last iteration.                           |
742|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
743|| `loop.length`         | The number of items in the sequence.              |
744|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
745|| `loop.cycle`          | A helper function to cycle between a list of      |
746||                       | sequences.  See the explanation below.            |
747|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
748|| `loop.depth`          | Indicates how deep in a recursive loop            |
749||                       | the rendering currently is.  Starts at level 1    |
750|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
751|| `loop.depth0`         | Indicates how deep in a recursive loop            |
752||                       | the rendering currently is.  Starts at level 0    |
753|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
754|| `loop.previtem`       | The item from the previous iteration of the loop. |
755||                       | Undefined during the first iteration.             |
756|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
757|| `loop.nextitem`       | The item from the following iteration of the loop.|
758||                       | Undefined during the last iteration.              |
759|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
760|| `loop.changed(*val)`  | True if previously called with a different value  |
761||                       | (or not called at all).                           |
762|+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
763|
764|Within a for-loop, it's possible to cycle among a list of strings/variables
765|each time through the loop by using the special `loop.cycle` helper::
766|
767|    {% for row in rows %}
768|        <li class="{{ loop.cycle('odd', 'even') }}">{{ row }}</li>
769|    {% endfor %}
770|
771|Since Jinja 2.1, an extra `cycle` helper exists that allows loop-unbound
772|cycling.  For more information, have a look at the :ref:`builtin-globals`.
773|
774|.. _loop-filtering:
775|
776|Unlike in Python, it's not possible to `break` or `continue` in a loop.  You
777|can, however, filter the sequence during iteration, which allows you to skip
778|items.  The following example skips all the users which are hidden::
779|
780|    {% for user in users if not user.hidden %}
781|        <li>{{ user.username|e }}</li>
782|    {% endfor %}
783|
784|The advantage is that the special `loop` variable will count correctly; thus
785|not counting the users not iterated over.
786|
787|If no iteration took place because the sequence was empty or the filtering
788|removed all the items from the sequence, you can render a default block
789|by using `else`::
790|
791|    <ul>
792|    {% for user in users %}
793|        <li>{{ user.username|e }}</li>
794|    {% else %}
795|        <li><em>no users found</em></li>
796|    {% endfor %}
797|    </ul>
798|
799|Note that, in Python, `else` blocks are executed whenever the corresponding
800|loop **did not** `break`.  Since Jinja loops cannot `break` anyway,
801|a slightly different behavior of the `else` keyword was chosen.
802|
803|It is also possible to use loops recursively.  This is useful if you are
804|dealing with recursive data such as sitemaps or RDFa.
805|To use loops recursively, you basically have to add the `recursive` modifier
806|to the loop definition and call the `loop` variable with the new iterable
807|where you want to recurse.
808|
809|The following example implements a sitemap with recursive loops::
810|
811|    <ul class="sitemap">
812|    {%- for item in sitemap recursive %}
813|        <li><a href="{{ item.href|e }}">{{ item.title }}</a>
814|        {%- if item.children -%}
815|            <ul class="submenu">{{ loop(item.children) }}</ul>
816|        {%- endif %}</li>
817|    {%- endfor %}
818|    </ul>
819|
820|The `loop` variable always refers to the closest (innermost) loop. If we
821|have more than one level of loops, we can rebind the variable `loop` by
822|writing `{% set outer_loop = loop %}` after the loop that we want to
823|use recursively. Then, we can call it using `{{ outer_loop(...) }}`
824|
825|Please note that assignments in loops will be cleared at the end of the
826|iteration and cannot outlive the loop scope.  Older versions of Jinja had
827|a bug where in some circumstances it appeared that assignments would work.
828|This is not supported.  See :ref:`assignments` for more information about
829|how to deal with this.
830|
831|If all you want to do is check whether some value has changed since the
832|last iteration or will change in the next iteration, you can use `previtem`
833|and `nextitem`::
834|
835|    {% for value in values %}
836|        {% if loop.previtem is defined and value > loop.previtem %}
837|            The value just increased!
838|        {% endif %}
839|        {{ value }}
840|        {% if loop.nextitem is defined and loop.nextitem > value %}
841|            The value will increase even more!
842|        {% endif %}
843|    {% endfor %}
844|
845|If you only care whether the value changed at all, using `changed` is even
846|easier::
847|
848|    {% for entry in entries %}
849|        {% if loop.changed(entry.category) %}
850|            <h2>{{ entry.category }}</h2>
851|        {% endif %}
852|        <p>{{ entry.message }}</p>
853|    {% endfor %}
854|
855|.. _if:
856|
857|If
858|~~
859|
860|The `if` statement in Jinja is comparable with the Python if statement.
861|In the simplest form, you can use it to test if a variable is defined, not
862|empty and not false::
863|
864|    {% if users %}
865|    <ul>
866|    {% for user in users %}
867|        <li>{{ user.username|e }}</li>
868|    {% endfor %}
869|    </ul>
870|    {% endif %}
871|
872|For multiple branches, `elif` and `else` can be used like in Python.  You can
873|use more complex :ref:`expressions` there, too::
874|
875|    {% if kenny.sick %}
876|        Kenny is sick.
877|    {% elif kenny.dead %}
878|        You killed Kenny!  You bastard!!!
879|    {% else %}
880|        Kenny looks okay --- so far
881|    {% endif %}
882|
883|If can also be used as an :ref:`inline expression <if-expression>` and for
884|:ref:`loop filtering <loop-filtering>`.
885|
886|.. _macros:
887|
888|Macros
889|~~~~~~
890|
891|Macros are comparable with functions in regular programming languages.  They
892|are useful to put often used idioms into reusable functions to not repeat
893|yourself ("DRY").
894|
895|Here's a small example of a macro that renders a form element::
896|
897|    {% macro input(name, value='', type='text', size=20) -%}
898|        <input type="{{ type }}" name="{{ name }}" value="{{
899|            value|e }}" size="{{ size }}">
900|    {%- endmacro %}
901|
902|The macro can then be called like a function in the namespace::
903|
904|    <p>{{ input('username') }}</p>
905|    <p>{{ input('password', type='password') }}</p>
906|
907|If the macro was defined in a different template, you have to
908|:ref:`import <import>` it first.
909|
910|Inside macros, you have access to three special variables:
911|
912|`varargs`
913|    If more positional arguments are passed to the macro than accepted by the
914|    macro, they end up in the special `varargs` variable as a list of values.
915|
916|`kwargs`
917|    Like `varargs` but for keyword arguments.  All unconsumed keyword
918|    arguments are stored in this special variable.
919|
920|`caller`
921|    If the macro was called from a :ref:`call<call>` tag, the caller is stored
922|    in this variable as a callable macro.
923|
924|Macros also expose some of their internal details.  The following attributes
925|are available on a macro object:
926|
927|`name`
928|    The name of the macro.  ``{{ input.name }}`` will print ``input``.
929|
930|`arguments`
931|    A tuple of the names of arguments the macro accepts.
932|
933|`catch_kwargs`
934|    This is `true` if the macro accepts extra keyword arguments (i.e.: accesses
935|    the special `kwargs` variable).
936|
937|`catch_varargs`
938|    This is `true` if the macro accepts extra positional arguments (i.e.:
939|    accesses the special `varargs` variable).
940|
941|`caller`
942|    This is `true` if the macro accesses the special `caller` variable and may
943|    be called from a :ref:`call<call>` tag.
944|
945|If a macro name starts with an underscore, it's not exported and can't
946|be imported.
947|
948|Due to how scopes work in Jinja, a macro in a child template does not
949|override a macro in a parent template. The following will output
950|"LAYOUT", not "CHILD".
951|
952|.. code-block:: jinja
953|    :caption: ``layout.txt``
954|
955|    {% macro foo() %}LAYOUT{% endmacro %}
956|    {% block body %}{% endblock %}
957|
958|.. code-block:: jinja
959|    :caption: ``child.txt``
960|
961|    {% extends 'layout.txt' %}
962|    {% macro foo() %}CHILD{% endmacro %}
963|    {% block body %}{{ foo() }}{% endblock %}
964|
965|
966|.. _call:
967|
968|Call
969|~~~~
970|
971|In some cases it can be useful to pass a macro to another macro.  For this
972|purpose, you can use the special `call` block.  The following example shows
973|a macro that takes advantage of the call functionality and how it can be
974|used::
975|
976|    {% macro render_dialog(title, class='dialog') -%}
977|        <div class="{{ class }}">
978|            <h2>{{ title }}</h2>
979|            <div class="contents">
980|                {{ caller() }}
981|            </div>
982|        </div>
983|    {%- endmacro %}
984|
985|    {% call render_dialog('Hello World') %}
986|        This is a simple dialog rendered by using a macro and
987|        a call block.
988|    {% endcall %}
989|
990|It's also possible to pass arguments back to the call block.  This makes it
991|useful as a replacement for loops.  Generally speaking, a call block works
992|exactly like a macro without a name.
993|
994|Here's an example of how a call block can be used with arguments::
995|
996|    {% macro dump_users(users) -%}
997|        <ul>
998|        {%- for user in users %}
999|            <li><p>{{ user.username|e }}</p>{{ caller(user) }}</li>
1000|        {%- endfor %}
1001|        </ul>
1002|    {%- endmacro %}
1003|
1004|    {% call(user) dump_users(list_of_user) %}
1005|        <dl>
1006|            <dt>Realname</dt>
1007|            <dd>{{ user.realname|e }}</dd>
1008|            <dt>Description</dt>
1009|            <dd>{{ user.description }}</dd>
1010|        </dl>
1011|    {% endcall %}
1012|
1013|
1014|Filters
1015|~~~~~~~
1016|
1017|Filter sections allow you to apply regular Jinja filters on a block of
1018|template data.  Just wrap the code in the special `filter` section::
1019|
1020|    {% filter upper %}
1021|        This text becomes uppercase
1022|    {% endfilter %}
1023|
1024|Filters that accept arguments can be called like this::
1025|
1026|    {% filter center(100) %}Center this{% endfilter %}
1027|
1028|.. _assignments:
1029|
1030|Assignments
1031|~~~~~~~~~~~
1032|
1033|Inside code blocks, you can also assign values to variables.  Assignments at
1034|top level (outside of blocks, macros or loops) are exported from the template
1035|like top level macros and can be imported by other templates.
1036|
1037|Assignments use the `set` tag and can have multiple targets::
1038|
1039|    {% set navigation = [('index.html', 'Index'), ('about.html', 'About')] %}
1040|    {% set key, value = call_something() %}
1041|
1042|.. admonition:: Scoping Behavior
1043|
1044|    Please keep in mind that it is not possible to set variables inside a
1045|    block and have them show up outside of it.  This also applies to
1046|    loops.  The only exception to that rule are if statements which do not
1047|    introduce a scope.  As a result the following template is not going
1048|    to do what you might expect::
1049|
1050|        {% set iterated = false %}
1051|        {% for item in seq %}
1052|            {{ item }}
1053|            {% set iterated = true %}
1054|        {% endfor %}
1055|        {% if not iterated %} did not iterate {% endif %}
1056|
1057|    It is not possible with Jinja syntax to do this.  Instead use
1058|    alternative constructs like the loop else block or the special `loop`
1059|    variable::
1060|
1061|        {% for item in seq %}
1062|            {{ item }}
1063|        {% else %}
1064|            did not iterate
1065|        {% endfor %}
1066|
1067|    As of version 2.10 more complex use cases can be handled using namespace
1068|    objects which allow propagating of changes across scopes::
1069|
1070|        {% set ns = namespace(found=false) %}
1071|        {% for item in items %}
1072|            {% if item.check_something() %}
1073|                {% set ns.found = true %}
1074|            {% endif %}
1075|            * {{ item.title }}
1076|        {% endfor %}
1077|        Found item having something: {{ ns.found }}
1078|
1079|    Note that the ``obj.attr`` notation in the `set` tag is only allowed for
1080|    namespace objects; attempting to assign an attribute on any other object
1081|    will raise an exception.
1082|
1083|    .. versionadded:: 2.10 Added support for namespace objects
1084|
1085|
1086|Block Assignments
1087|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1088|
1089|It's possible to use `set` as a block to assign the content of the block to a
1090|variable. This can be used to create multi-line strings, since Jinja doesn't
1091|support Python's triple quotes (``"""``, ``'''``).
1092|
1093|Instead of using an equals sign and a value, you only write the variable name,
1094|and everything until ``{% endset %}`` is captured.
1095|
1096|.. code-block:: jinja
1097|
1098|    {% set navigation %}
1099|        <li><a href="/">Index</a>
1100|        <li><a href="/downloads">Downloads</a>
1101|    {% endset %}
1102|
1103|Filters applied to the variable name will be applied to the block's content.
1104|
1105|.. code-block:: jinja
1106|
1107|    {% set reply | wordwrap %}
1108|        You wrote:
1109|        {{ message }}
1110|    {% endset %}
1111|
1112|.. versionadded:: 2.8
1113|
1114|.. versionchanged:: 2.10
1115|
1116|    Block assignment supports filters.
1117|
1118|.. _extends:
1119|
1120|Extends
1121|~~~~~~~
1122|
1123|The `extends` tag can be used to extend one template from another.  You can
1124|have multiple `extends` tags in a file, but only one of them may be executed at
1125|a time.
1126|
1127|See the section about :ref:`template-inheritance` above.
1128|
1129|
1130|.. _blocks:
1131|
1132|Blocks
1133|~~~~~~
1134|
1135|Blocks are used for inheritance and act as both placeholders and replacements
1136|at the same time.  They are documented in detail in the
1137|:ref:`template-inheritance` section.
1138|
1139|
1140|Include
1141|~~~~~~~
1142|
1143|The ``include`` tag renders another template and outputs the result into
1144|the current template.
1145|
1146|.. code-block:: jinja
1147|
1148|    {% include 'header.html' %}
1149|    Body goes here.
1150|    {% include 'footer.html' %}
1151|
1152|The included template has access to context of the current template by
1153|default. Use ``without context`` to use a separate context instead.
1154|``with context`` is also valid, but is the default behavior. See
1155|:ref:`import-visibility`.
1156|
1157|The included template can ``extend`` another template and override
1158|blocks in that template. However, the current template cannot override
1159|any blocks that the included template outputs.
1160|
1161|Use ``ignore missing`` to ignore the statement if the template does not
1162|exist. It must be placed *before* a context visibility statement.
1163|
1164|.. code-block:: jinja
1165|
1166|    {% include "sidebar.html" without context %}
1167|    {% include "sidebar.html" ignore missing %}
1168|    {% include "sidebar.html" ignore missing with context %}
1169|    {% include "sidebar.html" ignore missing without context %}
1170|
1171|If a list of templates is given, each will be tried in order until one
1172|is not missing. This can be used with ``ignore missing`` to ignore if
1173|none of the templates exist.
1174|
1175|.. code-block:: jinja
1176|
1177|    {% include ['page_detailed.html', 'page.html'] %}
1178|    {% include ['special_sidebar.html', 'sidebar.html'] ignore missing %}
1179|
1180|A variable, with either a template name or template object, can also be
1181|passed to the statement.
1182|
1183|.. _import:
1184|
1185|Import
1186|~~~~~~
1187|
1188|Jinja supports putting often used code into macros.  These macros can go into
1189|different templates and get imported from there.  This works similarly to the
1190|import statements in Python.  It's important to know that imports are cached
1191|and imported templates don't have access to the current template variables,
1192|just the globals by default.  For more details about context behavior of
1193|imports and includes, see :ref:`import-visibility`.
1194|
1195|There are two ways to import templates.  You can import a complete template
1196|into a variable or request specific macros / exported variables from it.
1197|
1198|Imagine we have a helper module that renders forms (called `forms.html`)::
1199|
1200|    {% macro input(name, value='', type='text') -%}
1201|        <input type="{{ type }}" value="{{ value|e }}" name="{{ name }}">
1202|    {%- endmacro %}
1203|
1204|    {%- macro textarea(name, value='', rows=10, cols=40) -%}
1205|        <textarea name="{{ name }}" rows="{{ rows }}" cols="{{ cols
1206|            }}">{{ value|e }}</textarea>
1207|    {%- endmacro %}
1208|
1209|The easiest and most flexible way to access a template's variables
1210|and macros is to import the whole template module into a variable.
1211|That way, you can access the attributes::
1212|
1213|    {% import 'forms.html' as forms %}
1214|    <dl>
1215|        <dt>Username</dt>
1216|        <dd>{{ forms.input('username') }}</dd>
1217|        <dt>Password</dt>
1218|        <dd>{{ forms.input('password', type='password') }}</dd>
1219|    </dl>
1220|    <p>{{ forms.textarea('comment') }}</p>
1221|
1222|
1223|Alternatively, you can import specific names from a template into the current
1224|namespace::
1225|
1226|    {% from 'forms.html' import input as input_field, textarea %}
1227|    <dl>
1228|        <dt>Username</dt>
1229|        <dd>{{ input_field('username') }}</dd>
1230|        <dt>Password</dt>
1231|        <dd>{{ input_field('password', type='password') }}</dd>
1232|    </dl>
1233|    <p>{{ textarea('comment') }}</p>
1234|
1235|Macros and variables starting with one or more underscores are private and
1236|cannot be imported.
1237|
1238|.. versionchanged:: 2.4
1239|   If a template object was passed to the template context, you can
1240|   import from that object.
1241|
1242|
1243|.. _import-visibility:
1244|
1245|Import Context Behavior
1246|-----------------------
1247|
1248|By default, included templates are passed the current context and imported
1249|templates are not.  The reason for this is that imports, unlike includes,
1250|are cached; as imports are often used just as a module that holds macros.
1251|
1252|This behavior can be changed explicitly: by adding `with context`
1253|or `without context` to the import/include directive, the current context
1254|can be passed to the template and caching is disabled automatically.
1255|
1256|Here are two examples::
1257|
1258|    {% from 'forms.html' import input with context %}
1259|    {% include 'header.html' without context %}
1260|
1261|.. admonition:: Note
1262|
1263|    In Jinja 2.0, the context that was passed to the included template
1264|    did not include variables defined in the template.  As a matter of
1265|    fact, this did not work::
1266|
1267|        {% for box in boxes %}
1268|            {% include "render_box.html" %}
1269|        {% endfor %}
1270|
1271|    The included template ``render_box.html`` is *not* able to access
1272|    `box` in Jinja 2.0. As of Jinja 2.1, ``render_box.html`` *is* able
1273|    to do so.
1274|
1275|
1276|.. _expressions:
1277|
1278|Expressions
1279|-----------
1280|
1281|Jinja allows basic expressions everywhere.  These work very similarly to
1282|regular Python; even if you're not working with Python
1283|you should feel comfortable with it.
1284|
1285|Literals
1286|~~~~~~~~
1287|
1288|The simplest form of expressions are literals.  Literals are representations
1289|for Python objects such as strings and numbers.  The following literals exist:
1290|
1291|``"Hello World"``
1292|    Everything between two double or single quotes is a string.  They are
1293|    useful whenever you need a string in the template (e.g. as
1294|    arguments to function calls and filters, or just to extend or include a
1295|    template).
1296|
1297|``42`` / ``123_456``
1298|    Integers are whole numbers without a decimal part. The '_' character
1299|    can be used to separate groups for legibility.
1300|
1301|``42.23`` / ``42.1e2`` / ``123_456.789``
1302|    Floating point numbers can be written using a '.' as a decimal mark.
1303|    They can also be written in scientific notation with an upper or
1304|    lower case 'e' to indicate the exponent part. The '_' character can
1305|    be used to separate groups for legibility, but cannot be used in the
1306|    exponent part.
1307|
1308|``['list', 'of', 'objects']``
1309|    Everything between two brackets is a list.  Lists are useful for storing
1310|    sequential data to be iterated over.  For example, you can easily
1311|    create a list of links using lists and tuples for (and with) a for loop::
1312|
1313|        <ul>
1314|        {% for href, caption in [('index.html', 'Index'), ('about.html', 'About'),
1315|                                 ('downloads.html', 'Downloads')] %}
1316|            <li><a href="{{ href }}">{{ caption }}</a></li>
1317|        {% endfor %}
1318|        </ul>
1319|
1320|``('tuple', 'of', 'values')``
1321|    Tuples are like lists that cannot be modified ("immutable").  If a tuple
1322|    only has one item, it must be followed by a comma (``('1-tuple',)``).
1323|    Tuples are usually used to represent items of two or more elements.
1324|    See the list example above for more details.
1325|
1326|``{'dict': 'of', 'key': 'and', 'value': 'pairs'}``
1327|    A dict in Python is a structure that combines keys and values.  Keys must
1328|    be unique and always have exactly one value.  Dicts are rarely used in
1329|    templates; they are useful in some rare cases such as the :func:`xmlattr`
1330|    filter.
1331|
1332|``true`` / ``false``
1333|    ``true`` is always true and ``false`` is always false.
1334|
1335|.. admonition:: Note
1336|
1337|    The special constants `true`, `false`, and `none` are indeed lowercase.
1338|    Because that caused confusion in the past, (`True` used to expand
1339|    to an undefined variable that was considered false),
1340|    all three can now also be written in title case
1341|    (`True`, `False`, and `None`).
1342|    However, for consistency, (all Jinja identifiers are lowercase)
1343|    you should use the lowercase versions.
1344|
1345|Math
1346|~~~~
1347|
1348|Jinja allows you to calculate with values.  This is rarely useful in templates
1349|but exists for completeness' sake.  The following operators are supported:
1350|
1351|``+``
1352|    Adds two objects together. Usually the objects are numbers, but if both are
1353|    strings or lists, you can concatenate them this way.  This, however, is not
1354|    the preferred way to concatenate strings!  For string concatenation, have
1355|    a look-see at the ``~`` operator.  ``{{ 1 + 1 }}`` is ``2``.
1356|
1357|``-``
1358|    Subtract the second number from the first one.  ``{{ 3 - 2 }}`` is ``1``.
1359|
1360|``/``
1361|    Divide two numbers.  The return value will be a floating point number.
1362|    ``{{ 1 / 2 }}`` is ``{{ 0.5 }}``.
1363|
1364|``//``
1365|    Divide two numbers and return the truncated integer result.
1366|    ``{{ 20 // 7 }}`` is ``2``.
1367|
1368|``%``
1369|    Calculate the remainder of an integer division.  ``{{ 11 % 7 }}`` is ``4``.
1370|
1371|``*``
1372|    Multiply the left operand with the right one.  ``{{ 2 * 2 }}`` would
1373|    return ``4``.  This can also be used to repeat a string multiple times.
1374|    ``{{ '=' * 80 }}`` would print a bar of 80 equal signs.
1375|
1376|``**``
1377|    Raise the left operand to the power of the right operand.
1378|    ``{{ 2**3 }}`` would return ``8``.
1379|
1380|    Unlike Python, chained pow is evaluated left to right.
1381|    ``{{ 3**3**3 }}`` is evaluated as ``(3**3)**3`` in Jinja, but would
1382|    be evaluated as ``3**(3**3)`` in Python. Use parentheses in Jinja
1383|    to be explicit about what order you want. It is usually preferable
1384|    to do extended math in Python and pass the results to ``render``
1385|    rather than doing it in the template.
1386|
1387|    This behavior may be changed in the future to match Python, if it's
1388|    possible to introduce an upgrade path.
1389|
1390|
1391|Comparisons
1392|~~~~~~~~~~~
1393|
1394|``==``
1395|    Compares two objects for equality.
1396|
1397|``!=``
1398|    Compares two objects for inequality.
1399|
1400|``>``
1401|    ``true`` if the left hand side is greater than the right hand side.
1402|
1403|``>=``
1404|    ``true`` if the left hand side is greater or equal to the right hand side.
1405|
1406|``<``
1407|    ``true`` if the left hand side is lower than the right hand side.
1408|
1409|``<=``
1410|    ``true`` if the left hand side is lower or equal to the right hand side.
1411|
1412|Logic
1413|~~~~~
1414|
1415|For ``if`` statements, ``for`` filtering, and ``if`` expressions, it can be
1416|useful to combine multiple expressions.
1417|
1418|``and``
1419|    For ``x and y``, if ``x`` is false, then the value is ``x``, else ``y``. In
1420|    a boolean context, this will be treated as ``True`` if both operands are
1421|    truthy.
1422|
1423|``or``
1424|    For ``x or y``, if ``x`` is true, then the value is ``x``, else ``y``. In a
1425|    boolean context, this will be treated as ``True`` if at least one operand is
1426|    truthy.
1427|
1428|``not``
1429|    For ``not x``, if ``x`` is false, then the value is ``True``, else
1430|    ``False``.
1431|
1432|    Prefer negating ``is`` and ``in`` using their infix notation:
1433|    ``foo is not bar`` instead of ``not foo is bar``; ``foo not in bar`` instead
1434|    of ``not foo in bar``. All other expressions require prefix notation:
1435|    ``not (foo and bar).``
1436|
1437|``(expr)``
1438|    Parentheses group an expression. This is used to change evaluation order, or
1439|    to make a long expression easier to read or less ambiguous.
1440|
1441|
1442|Other Operators
1443|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1444|
1445|The following operators are very useful but don't fit into any of the other
1446|two categories:
1447|
1448|``in``
1449|    Perform a sequence / mapping containment test.  Returns true if the left
1450|    operand is contained in the right.  ``{{ 1 in [1, 2, 3] }}`` would, for
1451|    example, return true.
1452|
1453|``is``
1454|    Performs a :ref:`test <tests>`.
1455|
1456|``|`` (pipe, vertical bar)
1457|    Applies a :ref:`filter <filters>`.
1458|
1459|``~`` (tilde)
1460|    Converts all operands into strings and concatenates them.
1461|
1462|    ``{{ "Hello " ~ name ~ "!" }}`` would return (assuming `name` is set
1463|    to ``'John'``) ``Hello John!``.
1464|
1465|``()``
1466|    Call a callable: ``{{ post.render() }}``.  Inside of the parentheses you
1467|    can use positional arguments and keyword arguments like in Python:
1468|
1469|    ``{{ post.render(user, full=true) }}``.
1470|
1471|``.`` / ``[]``
1472|    Get an attribute of an object.  (See :ref:`variables`)
1473|
1474|
1475|.. _if-expression:
1476|
1477|If Expression
1478|~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1479|
1480|It is also possible to use inline `if` expressions.  These are useful in some
1481|situations.  For example, you can use this to extend from one template if a
1482|variable is defined, otherwise from the default layout template::
1483|
1484|    {% extends layout_template if layout_template is defined else 'default.html' %}
1485|
1486|The general syntax is ``<do something> if <something is true> else <do
1487|something else>``.
1488|
1489|The `else` part is optional.  If not provided, the else block implicitly
1490|evaluates into an :class:`Undefined` object (regardless of what ``undefined``
1491|in the environment is set to):
1492|
1493|.. code-block:: jinja
1494|
1495|    {{ "[{}]".format(page.title) if page.title }}
1496|
1497|
1498|.. _python-methods:
1499|
1500|Python Methods
1501|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1502|
1503|You can also use any of the methods defined on a variable's type.
1504|The value returned from the method invocation is used as the value of the expression.
1505|Here is an example that uses methods defined on strings (where ``page.title`` is a string):
1506|
1507|.. code-block:: text
1508|
1509|    {{ page.title.capitalize() }}
1510|
1511|This works for methods on user-defined types. For example, if variable
1512|``f`` of type ``Foo`` has a method ``bar`` defined on it, you can do the
1513|following:
1514|
1515|.. code-block:: text
1516|
1517|    {{ f.bar(value) }}
1518|
1519|Operator methods also work as expected. For example, ``%`` implements
1520|printf-style for strings:
1521|
1522|.. code-block:: text
1523|
1524|    {{ "Hello, %s!" % name }}
1525|
1526|Although you should prefer the ``.format`` method for that case (which
1527|is a bit contrived in the context of rendering a template):
1528|
1529|.. code-block:: text
1530|
1531|    {{ "Hello, {}!".format(name) }}
1532|
1533|

1554|.. _builtin-globals:
1555|
1556|List of Global Functions
1557|------------------------
1558|
1559|The following functions are available in the global scope by default:
1560|
1561|.. py:currentmodule:: jinja-globals
1562|
1563|.. function:: range([start,] stop[, step])
1564|
1565|    Return a list containing an arithmetic progression of integers.
1566|    ``range(i, j)`` returns ``[i, i+1, i+2, ..., j-1]``;
1567|    start (!) defaults to ``0``.
1568|    When step is given, it specifies the increment (or decrement).
1569|    For example, ``range(4)`` and ``range(0, 4, 1)`` return ``[0, 1, 2, 3]``.
1570|    The end point is omitted!
1571|    These are exactly the valid indices for a list of 4 elements.
1572|
1573|    This is useful to repeat a template block multiple times, e.g.
1574|    to fill a list.  Imagine you have 7 users in the list but you want to
1575|    render three empty items to enforce a height with CSS::
1576|
1577|        <ul>
1578|        {% for user in users %}
1579|            <li>{{ user.username }}</li>
1580|        {% endfor %}
1581|        {% for number in range(10 - users|count) %}
1582|            <li class="empty"><span>...</span></li>
1583|        {% endfor %}
1584|        </ul>
1585|
1586|.. function:: lipsum(n=5, html=True, min=20, max=100)
1587|
1588|    Generates some lorem ipsum for the template.  By default, five paragraphs
1589|    of HTML are generated with each paragraph between 20 and 100 words.
1590|    If html is False, regular text is returned.  This is useful to generate simple
1591|    contents for layout testing.
1592|
1593|.. function:: dict(\**items)
1594|
1595|    A convenient alternative to dict literals.  ``{'foo': 'bar'}`` is the same
1596|    as ``dict(foo='bar')``.
1597|
1598|.. class:: cycler(\*items)
1599|
1600|    Cycle through values by yielding them one at a time, then restarting
1601|    once the end is reached.
1602|
1603|    Similar to ``loop.cycle``, but can be used outside loops or across
1604|    multiple loops. For example, render a list of folders and files in a
1605|    list, alternating giving them "odd" and "even" classes.
1606|
1607|    .. code-block:: html+jinja
1608|
1609|        {% set row_class = cycler("odd", "even") %}
1610|        <ul class="browser">
1611|        {% for folder in folders %}
1612|          <li class="folder {{ row_class.next() }}">{{ folder }}
1613|        {% endfor %}
1614|        {% for file in files %}
1615|          <li class="file {{ row_class.next() }}">{{ file }}
1616|        {% endfor %}
1617|        </ul>
1618|
1619|    :param items: Each positional argument will be yielded in the order
1620|        given for each cycle.
1621|
1622|    .. versionadded:: 2.1
1623|
1624|    .. property:: current
1625|
1626|        Return the current item. Equivalent to the item that will be
1627|        returned next time :meth:`next` is called.
1628|
1629|    .. method:: next()
1630|
1631|        Return the current item, then advance :attr:`current` to the
1632|        next item.
1633|
1634|    .. method:: reset()
1635|
1636|        Resets the current item to the first item.
1637|
1638|.. class:: joiner(sep=', ')
1639|
1640|    A tiny helper that can be used to "join" multiple sections.  A joiner is
1641|    passed a string and will return that string every time it's called, except
1642|    the first time (in which case it returns an empty string).  You can
1643|    use this to join things::
1644|
1645|        {% set pipe = joiner("|") %}
1646|        {% if categories %} {{ pipe() }}
1647|            Categories: {{ categories|join(", ") }}
1648|        {% endif %}
1649|        {% if author %} {{ pipe() }}
1650|            Author: {{ author() }}
1651|        {% endif %}
1652|        {% if can_edit %} {{ pipe() }}
1653|            <a href="?action=edit">Edit</a>
1654|        {% endif %}
1655|
1656|    .. versionadded:: 2.1
1657|
1658|.. class:: namespace(...)
1659|
1660|    Creates a new container that allows attribute assignment using the
1661|    ``{% set %}`` tag::
1662|
1663|        {% set ns = namespace() %}
1664|        {% set ns.foo = 'bar' %}
1665|
1666|    The main purpose of this is to allow carrying a value from within a loop
1667|    body to an outer scope.  Initial values can be provided as a dict, as
1668|    keyword arguments, or both (same behavior as Python's `dict` constructor)::
1669|
1670|        {% set ns = namespace(found=false) %}
1671|        {% for item in items %}
1672|            {% if item.check_something() %}
1673|                {% set ns.found = true %}
1674|            {% endif %}
1675|            * {{ item.title }}
1676|        {% endfor %}
1677|        Found item having something: {{ ns.found }}
1678|
1679|    .. versionadded:: 2.10
1680|
1681|    .. versionchanged:: 3.2
1682|        Namespace attributes can be assigned to in multiple assignment.
1683|

1685|Extensions
1686|----------
1687|
1688|.. py:currentmodule:: jinja2
1689|
1690|The following sections cover the built-in Jinja extensions that may be
1691|enabled by an application.  An application could also provide further
1692|extensions not covered by this documentation; in which case there should
1693|be a separate document explaining said :ref:`extensions
1694|<jinja-extensions>`.
1695|
1696|
1697|.. _i18n-in-templates:
1698|
1699|i18n
1700|~~~~
1701|
1702|If the :ref:`i18n-extension` is enabled, it's possible to mark text in
1703|the template as translatable. To mark a section as translatable, use a
1704|``trans`` block:
1705|
1706|.. code-block:: jinja
1707|
1708|    {% trans %}Hello, {{ user }}!{% endtrans %}
1709|
1710|Inside the block, no statements are allowed, only text and simple
1711|variable tags.
1712|
1713|Variable tags can only be a name, not attribute access, filters, or
1714|other expressions. To use an expression, bind it to a name in the
1715|``trans`` tag for use in the block.
1716|
1717|.. code-block:: jinja
1718|
1719|    {% trans user=user.username %}Hello, {{ user }}!{% endtrans %}
1720|
1721|To bind more than one expression, separate each with a comma (``,``).
1722|
1723|.. code-block:: jinja
1724|
1725|    {% trans book_title=book.title, author=author.name %}
1726|    This is {{ book_title }} by {{ author }}
1727|    {% endtrans %}
1728|
1729|To pluralize, specify both the singular and plural forms separated by
1730|the ``pluralize`` tag.
1731|
1732|.. code-block:: jinja
1733|
1734|    {% trans count=list|length %}
1735|    There is {{ count }} {{ name }} object.
1736|    {% pluralize %}
1737|    There are {{ count }} {{ name }} objects.
1738|    {% endtrans %}
1739|
1740|By default, the first variable in a block is used to determine whether
1741|to use singular or plural form. If that isn't correct, specify the
1742|variable used for pluralizing as a parameter to ``pluralize``.
1743|
1744|.. code-block:: jinja
1745|
1746|    {% trans ..., user_count=users|length %}...
1747|    {% pluralize user_count %}...{% endtrans %}
1748|
1749|When translating blocks of text, whitespace and linebreaks result in
1750|hard to read and error-prone translation strings. To avoid this, a trans
1751|block can be marked as trimmed, which will replace all linebreaks and
1752|the whitespace surrounding them with a single space and remove leading
1753|and trailing whitespace.
1754|
1755|.. code-block:: jinja
1756|
1757|    {% trans trimmed book_title=book.title %}
1758|        This is {{ book_title }}.
1759|        You should read it!
1760|    {% endtrans %}
1761|
1762|This results in ``This is %(book_title)s. You should read it!`` in the
1763|translation file.
1764|
1765|If trimming is enabled globally, the ``notrimmed`` modifier can be used
1766|to disable it for a block.
1767|
1768|.. versionadded:: 2.10
1769|   The ``trimmed`` and ``notrimmed`` modifiers have been added.
1770|
1771|If the translation depends on the context that the message appears in,
1772|the ``pgettext`` and ``npgettext`` functions take a ``context`` string
1773|as the first argument, which is used to select the appropriate
1774|translation. To specify a context with the ``{% trans %}`` tag, provide
1775|a string as the first token after ``trans``.
1776|
1777|.. code-block:: jinja
1778|
1779|    {% trans "fruit" %}apple{% endtrans %}
1780|    {% trans "fruit" trimmed count -%}
1781|        1 apple
1782|    {%- pluralize -%}
1783|        {{ count }} apples
1784|    {%- endtrans %}
1785|
1786|.. versionadded:: 3.1
1787|    A context can be passed to the ``trans`` tag to use ``pgettext`` and
1788|    ``npgettext``.
1789|
1790|It's possible to translate strings in expressions with these functions:
1791|
1792|-   ``_(message)``: Alias for ``gettext``.
1793|-   ``gettext(message)``: Translate a message.
1794|-   ``ngettext(singular, plural, n)``: Translate a singular or plural
1795|    message based on a count variable.
1796|-   ``pgettext(context, message)``: Like ``gettext()``, but picks the
1797|    translation based on the context string.
1798|-   ``npgettext(context, singular, plural, n)``: Like ``npgettext()``,
1799|    but picks the translation based on the context string.
1800|
1801|You can print a translated string like this:
1802|
1803|.. code-block:: jinja
1804|
1805|    {{ _("Hello, World!") }}
1806|
1807|To use placeholders, use the ``format`` filter.
1808|
1809|.. code-block:: jinja
1810|
1811|    {{ _("Hello, %(user)s!")|format(user=user.username) }}
1812|
1813|Always use keyword arguments to ``format``, as other languages may not
1814|use the words in the same order.
1815|
1816|If :ref:`newstyle-gettext` calls are activated, using placeholders is
1817|easier. Formatting is part of the ``gettext`` call instead of using the
1818|``format`` filter.
1819|
1820|.. sourcecode:: jinja
1821|
1822|    {{ gettext('Hello World!') }}
1823|    {{ gettext('Hello %(name)s!', name='World') }}
1824|    {{ ngettext('%(num)d apple', '%(num)d apples', apples|count) }}
1825|
1826|The ``ngettext`` function's format string automatically receives the
1827|count as a ``num`` parameter in addition to the given parameters.
1828|
1829|
1830|Expression Statement
1831|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1832|
1833|If the expression-statement extension is loaded, a tag called `do` is available
1834|that works exactly like the regular variable expression (``{{ ... }}``); except
1835|it doesn't print anything.  This can be used to modify lists::
1836|
1837|    {% do navigation.append('a string') %}
1838|
1839|
1840|Loop Controls
1841|~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1842|
1843|If the application enables the :ref:`loopcontrols-extension`, it's possible to
1844|use `break` and `continue` in loops.  When `break` is reached, the loop is
1845|terminated;  if `continue` is reached, the processing is stopped and continues
1846|with the next iteration.
1847|
1848|Here's a loop that skips every second item::
1849|
1850|    {% for user in users %}
1851|        {%- if loop.index is even %}{% continue %}{% endif %}
1852|        ...
1853|    {% endfor %}
1854|
1855|Likewise, a loop that stops processing after the 10th iteration::
1856|
1857|    {% for user in users %}
1858|        {%- if loop.index >= 10 %}{% break %}{% endif %}
1859|    {%- endfor %}
1860|
1861|Note that ``loop.index`` starts with 1, and ``loop.index0`` starts with 0
1862|(See: :ref:`for-loop`).
1863|
1864|
1865|Debug Statement
1866|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1867|
1868|If the :ref:`debug-extension` is enabled, a ``{% debug %}`` tag will be
1869|available to dump the current context as well as the available filters
1870|and tests. This is useful to see what's available to use in the template
1871|without setting up a debugger.
1872|
1873|.. code-block:: html+jinja
1874|
1875|    <pre>{% debug %}</pre>
1876|
1877|.. code-block:: text
1878|
1879|    {'context': {'cycler': <class 'jinja2.utils.Cycler'>,
1880|                 ...,
1881|                 'namespace': <class 'jinja2.utils.Namespace'>},
1882|     'filters': ['abs', 'attr', 'batch', 'capitalize', 'center', 'count', 'd',
1883|                 ..., 'urlencode', 'urlize', 'wordcount', 'wordwrap', 'xmlattr'],
1884|     'tests': ['!=', '<', '<=', '==', '>', '>=', 'callable', 'defined',
1885|               ..., 'odd', 'sameas', 'sequence', 'string', 'undefined', 'upper']}
1886|
1887|
1888|With Statement
1889|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1890|
1891|.. versionadded:: 2.3
1892|
1893|The with statement makes it possible to create a new inner scope.
1894|Variables set within this scope are not visible outside of the scope.
1895|
1896|With in a nutshell::
1897|
1898|    {% with %}
1899|        {% set foo = 42 %}
1900|        {{ foo }}           foo is 42 here
1901|    {% endwith %}
1902|    foo is not visible here any longer
1903|
1904|Because it is common to set variables at the beginning of the scope,
1905|you can do that within the `with` statement.  The following two examples
1906|are equivalent::
1907|
1908|    {% with foo = 42 %}
1909|        {{ foo }}
1910|    {% endwith %}
1911|
1912|    {% with %}
1913|        {% set foo = 42 %}
1914|        {{ foo }}
1915|    {% endwith %}
1916|
1917|An important note on scoping here.  In Jinja versions before 2.9 the
1918|behavior of referencing one variable to another had some unintended
1919|consequences.  In particular one variable could refer to another defined
1920|in the same with block's opening statement.  This caused issues with the
1921|cleaned up scoping behavior and has since been improved.  In particular
1922|in newer Jinja versions the following code always refers to the variable
1923|`a` from outside the `with` block::
1924|
1925|    {% with a={}, b=a.attribute %}...{% endwith %}
1926|
1927|In earlier Jinja versions the `b` attribute would refer to the results of
1928|the first attribute.  If you depend on this behavior you can rewrite it to
1929|use the ``set`` tag::
1930|
1931|    {% with a={} %}
1932|        {% set b = a.attribute %}
1933|    {% endwith %}
1934|
1935|.. admonition:: Extension
1936|
1937|   In older versions of Jinja (before 2.9) it was required to enable this
1938|   feature with an extension.  It's now enabled by default.
1939|
1940|.. _autoescape-overrides:
1941|
1942|Autoescape Overrides
1943|--------------------
1944|
1945|.. versionadded:: 2.4
1946|
1947|If you want you can activate and deactivate the autoescaping from within
1948|the templates.
1949|
1950|Example::
1951|
1952|    {% autoescape true %}
1953|        Autoescaping is active within this block
1954|    {% endautoescape %}
1955|
1956|    {% autoescape false %}
1957|        Autoescaping is inactive within this block
1958|    {% endautoescape %}
1959|
1960|After an `endautoescape` the behavior is reverted to what it was before.
1961|
1962|.. admonition:: Extension
1963|
1964|   In older versions of Jinja (before 2.9) it was required to enable this
1965|   feature with an extension.  It's now enabled by default.

1|API
2|===
3|
4|.. module:: jinja2
5|    :noindex:
6|    :synopsis: public Jinja API
7|
8|This document describes the API to Jinja and not the template language
9|(for that, see :doc:`/templates`). It will be most useful as reference
10|to those implementing the template interface to the application and not
11|those who are creating Jinja templates.
12|
13|Basics
14|------
15|
16|Jinja uses a central object called the template :class:`Environment`.
17|Instances of this class are used to store the configuration and global objects,
18|and are used to load templates from the file system or other locations.
19|Even if you are creating templates from strings by using the constructor of
20|:class:`Template` class, an environment is created automatically for you,
21|albeit a shared one.
22|
23|Most applications will create one :class:`Environment` object on application
24|initialization and use that to load templates.  In some cases however, it's
25|useful to have multiple environments side by side, if different configurations
26|are in use.
27|
28|The simplest way to configure Jinja to load templates for your
29|application is to use :class:`~loaders.PackageLoader`.
30|
31|.. code-block:: python
32|
33|    from jinja2 import Environment, PackageLoader, select_autoescape
34|    env = Environment(
35|        loader=PackageLoader("yourapp"),
36|        autoescape=select_autoescape()
37|    )
38|
39|This will create a template environment with a loader that looks up
40|templates in the ``templates`` folder inside the ``yourapp`` Python
41|package (or next to the ``yourapp.py`` Python module). It also enables
42|autoescaping for HTML files. This loader only requires that ``yourapp``
43|is importable, it figures out the absolute path to the folder for you.
44|
45|Different loaders are available to load templates in other ways or from
46|other locations. They're listed in the `Loaders`_ section below. You can
47|also write your own if you want to load templates from a source that's
48|more specialized to your project.
49|
50|To load a template from this environment, call the :meth:`get_template`
51|method, which returns the loaded :class:`Template`.
52|
53|.. code-block:: python
54|
55|    template = env.get_template("mytemplate.html")
56|
57|To render it with some variables, call the :meth:`render` method.
58|
59|.. code-block:: python
60|
61|    print(template.render(the="variables", go="here"))
62|
63|Using a template loader rather than passing strings to :class:`Template`
64|or :meth:`Environment.from_string` has multiple advantages.  Besides being
65|a lot easier to use it also enables template inheritance.
66|
67|.. admonition:: Notes on Autoescaping
68|
69|   In future versions of Jinja we might enable autoescaping by default
70|   for security reasons.  As such you are encouraged to explicitly
71|   configure autoescaping now instead of relying on the default.
72|
73|
74|High Level API
75|--------------
76|
77|The high-level API is the API you will use in the application to load and
78|render Jinja templates.  The :ref:`low-level-api` on the other side is only
79|useful if you want to dig deeper into Jinja or :ref:`develop extensions
80|<jinja-extensions>`.

223|Autoescaping
224|------------
225|
226|.. versionchanged:: 2.4
227|
228|Jinja now comes with autoescaping support.  As of Jinja 2.9 the
229|autoescape extension is removed and built-in.  However autoescaping is
230|not yet enabled by default though this will most likely change in the
231|future.  It's recommended to configure a sensible default for
232|autoescaping.  This makes it possible to enable and disable autoescaping
233|on a per-template basis (HTML versus text for instance).
234|
235|.. autofunction:: jinja2.select_autoescape
236|
237|Here a recommended setup that enables autoescaping for templates ending
238|in ``'.html'``, ``'.htm'`` and ``'.xml'`` and disabling it by default
239|for all other extensions.  You can use the :func:`~jinja2.select_autoescape`
240|function for this::
241|
242|    from jinja2 import Environment, PackageLoader, select_autoescape
243|    env = Environment(autoescape=select_autoescape(['html', 'htm', 'xml']),
244|                      loader=PackageLoader('mypackage'))
245|
246|The :func:`~jinja.select_autoescape` function returns a function that
247|works roughly like this::
248|
249|    def autoescape(template_name):
250|        if template_name is None:
251|            return False
252|        if template_name.endswith(('.html', '.htm', '.xml'))
253|
254|When implementing a guessing autoescape function, make sure you also
255|accept `None` as valid template name.  This will be passed when generating
256|templates from strings.  You should always configure autoescaping as
257|defaults in the future might change.
258|
259|Inside the templates the behaviour can be temporarily changed by using
260|the `autoescape` block (see :ref:`autoescape-overrides`).
261|
262|
263|.. _identifier-naming:
264|
265|Notes on Identifiers
266|--------------------
267|
268|Jinja uses Python naming rules. Valid identifiers can be any combination
269|of characters accepted by Python.
270|
271|Filters and tests are looked up in separate namespaces and have slightly
272|modified identifier syntax.  Filters and tests may contain dots to group
273|filters and tests by topic.  For example it's perfectly valid to add a
274|function into the filter dict and call it `to.str`.  The regular
275|expression for filter and test identifiers is
276|``[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*(\.[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*)*``.
277|
278|
279|Undefined Types
280|---------------
281|
282|These classes can be used as undefined types.  The :class:`Environment`
283|constructor takes an `undefined` parameter that can be one of those classes
284|or a custom subclass of :class:`Undefined`.  Whenever the template engine is
285|unable to look up a name or access an attribute one of those objects is
286|created and returned.  Some operations on undefined values are then allowed,
287|others fail.
288|
289|The closest to regular Python behavior is the :class:`StrictUndefined` which
290|disallows all operations beside testing if it's an undefined object.
291|

304|    .. attribute:: _undefined_name
305|
306|        The name for the undefined variable / attribute or just `None`
307|        if no such information exists.
308|
309|    .. attribute:: _undefined_exception
310|
311|        The exception that the undefined object wants to raise.  This
312|        is usually one of :exc:`UndefinedError` or :exc:`SecurityError`.
313|
314|    .. method:: _fail_with_undefined_error(\*args, \**kwargs)
315|
316|        When called with any arguments this method raises
317|        :attr:`_undefined_exception` with an error message generated
318|        from the undefined hints stored on the undefined object.
319|
320|.. autoclass:: jinja2.ChainableUndefined()
321|
322|.. autoclass:: jinja2.DebugUndefined()
323|
324|.. autoclass:: jinja2.StrictUndefined()
325|
326|There is also a factory function that can decorate undefined objects to
327|implement logging on failures:
328|
329|.. autofunction:: jinja2.make_logging_undefined
330|
331|Undefined objects are created by calling :attr:`undefined`.
332|
333|.. admonition:: Implementation
334|
335|    :class:`Undefined` is implemented by overriding the special
336|    ``__underscore__`` methods. For example the default
337|    :class:`Undefined` class implements ``__str__`` to returns an empty
338|    string, while ``__int__`` and others fail with an exception. To
339|    allow conversion to int by returning ``0`` you can implement your
340|    own subclass.
341|
342|    .. code-block:: python
343|
344|        class NullUndefined(Undefined):
345|            def __int__(self):
346|                return 0
347|
348|            def __float__(self):
349|                return 0.0
350|
351|    To disallow a method, override it and raise
352|    :attr:`~Undefined._undefined_exception`.  Because this is very
353|    common there is the helper method
354|    :meth:`~Undefined._fail_with_undefined_error` that raises the error
355|    with the correct information. Here's a class that works like the
356|    regular :class:`Undefined` but fails on iteration::
357|
358|        class NonIterableUndefined(Undefined):
359|            def __iter__(self):
360|                self._fail_with_undefined_error()
