363|The Context
364|-----------
365|
366|.. autoclass:: jinja2.runtime.Context()
367|    :members: get, resolve, resolve_or_missing, get_exported, get_all
368|
369|    .. attribute:: parent
370|
371|        A dict of read only, global variables the template looks up.  These
372|        can either come from another :class:`Context`, from the
373|        :attr:`Environment.globals` or :attr:`Template.globals` or points
374|        to a dict created by combining the globals with the variables
375|        passed to the render function.  It must not be altered.
376|
377|    .. attribute:: vars
378|
379|        The template local variables.  This list contains environment and
380|        context functions from the :attr:`parent` scope as well as local
381|        modifications and exported variables from the template.  The template
382|        will modify this dict during template evaluation but filters and
383|        context functions are not allowed to modify it.
384|
385|    .. attribute:: environment
386|
387|        The environment that loaded the template.
388|
389|    .. attribute:: exported_vars
390|
391|        This set contains all the names the template exports.  The values for
392|        the names are in the :attr:`vars` dict.  In order to get a copy of the
393|        exported variables as dict, :meth:`get_exported` can be used.
394|
395|    .. attribute:: name
396|
397|        The load name of the template owning this context.
398|
399|    .. attribute:: blocks
400|
401|        A dict with the current mapping of blocks in the template.  The keys
402|        in this dict are the names of the blocks, and the values a list of
403|        blocks registered.  The last item in each list is the current active
404|        block (latest in the inheritance chain).
405|
406|    .. attribute:: eval_ctx
407|
408|        The current :ref:`eval-context`.
409|
410|    .. automethod:: jinja2.runtime.Context.call(callable, \*args, \**kwargs)
411|
412|
413|The context is immutable, it prevents modifications, and if it is
414|modified somehow despite that those changes may not show up. For
415|performance, Jinja does not use the context as data storage for, only as
416|a primary data source. Variables that the template does not define are
417|looked up in the context, but variables the template does define are
418|stored locally.
419|
420|Instead of modifying the context directly, a function should return
421|a value that can be assigned to a variable within the template itself.

462|Bytecode Cache
463|--------------
464|
465|Jinja 2.1 and higher support external bytecode caching.  Bytecode caches make
466|it possible to store the generated bytecode on the file system or a different
467|location to avoid parsing the templates on first use.

469|This is especially useful if you have a web application that is initialized on
470|the first request and Jinja compiles many templates at once which slows down
471|the application.

502|Async Support
503|-------------
504|
505|.. versionadded:: 2.9
506|
507|Jinja supports the Python ``async`` and ``await`` syntax. For the
508|template designer, this support (when enabled) is entirely transparent,
509|templates continue to look exactly the same. However, developers should
510|be aware of the implementation as it affects what types of APIs you can
511|use.
512|
513|By default, async support is disabled. Enabling it will cause the
514|environment to compile different code behind the scenes in order to
515|handle async and sync code in an asyncio event loop. This has the
516|following implications:
517|
518|-   The compiled code uses ``await`` for functions and attributes, and
519|    uses ``async for`` loops. In order to support using both async and
520|    sync functions in this context, a small wrapper is placed around
521|    all calls and access, which adds overhead compared to purely async
522|    code.
523|-   Sync methods and filters become wrappers around their corresponding
524|    async implementations where needed. For example, ``render`` invokes
525|    ``async_render``, and ``|map`` supports async iterables.
526|
527|Awaitable objects can be returned from functions in templates and any
528|function call in a template will automatically await the result. The
529|``await`` you would normally add in Python is implied. For example, you
530|can provide a method that asynchronously loads data from a database, and
531|from the template designer's point of view it can be called like any
532|other function.
533|
534|
535|.. _policies:
536|
537|Policies
538|--------
539|
540|Starting with Jinja 2.9 policies can be configured on the environment
541|which can slightly influence how filters and other template constructs
542|behave.  They can be configured with the
543|:attr:`~jinja2.Environment.policies` attribute.
544|
545|Example::
546|
547|    env.policies['urlize.rel'] = 'nofollow noopener'
548|
549|``truncate.leeway``:
550|    Configures the leeway default for the `truncate` filter.  Leeway as
551|    introduced in 2.9 but to restore compatibility with older templates
552|    it can be configured to `0` to get the old behavior back.  The default
553|    is `5`.
554|
555|``urlize.rel``:
556|    A string that defines the items for the `rel` attribute of generated
557|    links with the `urlize` filter.  These items are always added.  The
558|    default is `noopener`.
559|
560|``urlize.target``:
561|    The default target that is issued for links from the `urlize` filter
562|    if no other target is defined by the call explicitly.
563|
564|``urlize.extra_schemes``:
565|    Recognize URLs that start with these schemes in addition to the
566|    default ``http://``, ``https://``, and ``mailto:``.
567|
568|``json.dumps_function``:
569|    If this is set to a value other than `None` then the `tojson` filter
570|    will dump with this function instead of the default one.  Note that
571|    this function should accept arbitrary extra arguments which might be
572|    passed in the future from the filter.  Currently the only argument
573|    that might be passed is `indent`.  The default dump function is
574|    ``json.dumps``.
575|
576|``json.dumps_kwargs``:
577|    Keyword arguments to be passed to the dump function.  The default is
578|    ``{'sort_keys': True}``.
579|
580|.. _ext-i18n-trimmed:
581|
582|``ext.i18n.trimmed``:
583|    If this is set to `True`, ``{% trans %}`` blocks of the
584|    :ref:`i18n-extension` will always unify linebreaks and surrounding
585|    whitespace as if the `trimmed` modifier was used.

640|.. _writing-filters:
641|
642|Custom Filters
643|--------------
644|
645|Filters are Python functions that take the value to the left of the
646|filter as the first argument and produce a new value. Arguments passed
647|to the filter are passed after the value.
648|
649|For example, the filter ``{{ 42|myfilter(23) }}`` is called behind the
650|scenes as ``myfilter(42, 23)``.
651|
652|Jinja comes with some :ref:`built-in filters <builtin-filters>`. To use
653|a custom filter, write a function that takes at least a ``value``
654|argument, then register it in :attr:`Environment.filters`.
655|
656|Here's a filter that formats datetime objects:
657|
658|.. code-block:: python
659|
660|    def datetime_format(value, format="%H:%M %d-%m-%y"):
661|        return value.strftime(format)
662|
663|    environment.filters["datetime_format"] = datetime_format
664|
665|Now it can be used in templates:
666|
667|.. sourcecode:: jinja
668|
669|    {{ article.pub_date|datetime_format }}
670|    {{ article.pub_date|datetime_format("%B %Y") }}
671|
672|Some decorators are available to tell Jinja to pass extra information to
673|the filter. The object is passed as the first argument, making the value
674|being filtered the second argument.
675|
676|-   :func:`pass_environment` passes the :class:`Environment`.
677|-   :func:`pass_eval_context` passes the :ref:`eval-context`.
678|-   :func:`pass_context` passes the current
679|    :class:`~jinja2.runtime.Context`.
680|
681|Here's a filter that converts line breaks into HTML ``<br>`` and ``<p>``
682|tags. It uses the eval context to check if autoescape is currently
683|enabled before escaping the input and marking the output safe.
684|
685|.. code-block:: python
686|
687|    import re
688|    from jinja2 import pass_eval_context
689|    from markupsafe import Markup, escape
690|
691|    @pass_eval_context
692|    def nl2br(eval_ctx, value):
693|        br = "<br>\n"
694|
695|        if eval_ctx.autoescape:
696|            value = escape(value)
697|            br = Markup(br)
698|
699|        result = "\n\n".join(
700|            f"<p>{br.join(p.splitlines())}</p>"
701|            for p in re.split(r"(?:\r\n|\r(?!\n)|\n){2,}", value)
702|        )
703|        return Markup(result) if eval_ctx.autoescape else result
704|
705|
706|.. _writing-tests:
707|
708|Custom Tests
709|------------
710|
711|Test are Python functions that take the value to the left of the test as
712|the first argument, and return ``True`` or ``False``. Arguments passed
713|to the test are passed after the value.
714|
715|For example, the test ``{{ 42 is even }}`` is called behind the scenes
716|as ``is_even(42)``.
717|
718|Jinja comes with some :ref:`built-in tests <builtin-tests>`. To use a
719|custom tests, write a function that takes at least a ``value`` argument,
720|then register it in :attr:`Environment.tests`.
721|
722|Here's a test that checks if a value is a prime number:
723|
724|.. code-block:: python
725|
726|    import math
727|
728|    def is_prime(n):
729|        if n == 2:
730|            return True
731|
732|        for i in range(2, int(math.ceil(math.sqrt(n))) + 1):
733|            if n % i == 0:
734|                return False
735|
736|        return True
737|
738|    environment.tests["prime"] = is_prime
739|
740|Now it can be used in templates:
741|
742|.. sourcecode:: jinja
743|
744|    {% if value is prime %}
745|        {{ value }} is a prime number
746|    {% else %}
747|        {{ value }} is not a prime number
748|    {% endif %}
749|
750|Some decorators are available to tell Jinja to pass extra information to
751|the test. The object is passed as the first argument, making the value
752|being tested the second argument.
753|
754|-   :func:`pass_environment` passes the :class:`Environment`.
755|-   :func:`pass_eval_context` passes the :ref:`eval-context`.
756|-   :func:`pass_context` passes the current
757|    :class:`~jinja2.runtime.Context`.
758|
759|
760|.. _eval-context:
761|
762|Evaluation Context
763|------------------
764|
765|The evaluation context (short eval context or eval ctx) makes it
766|possible to activate and deactivate compiled features at runtime.
767|
768|Currently it is only used to enable and disable automatic escaping, but
769|it can be used by extensions as well.
770|
771|The ``autoescape`` setting should be checked on the evaluation context,
772|not the environment. The evaluation context will have the computed value
773|for the current template.
774|
775|Instead of ``pass_environment``:
776|
777|.. code-block:: python
778|
779|    @pass_environment
780|    def filter(env, value):
781|        result = do_something(value)
782|
783|        if env.autoescape:
784|            result = Markup(result)
785|
786|        return result
787|
788|Use ``pass_eval_context`` if you only need the setting:
789|
790|.. code-block:: python
791|
792|    @pass_eval_context
793|    def filter(eval_ctx, value):
794|        result = do_something(value)
795|
796|        if eval_ctx.autoescape:
797|            result = Markup(result)
798|
799|        return result
800|
801|Or use ``pass_context`` if you need other context behavior as well:
802|
803|.. code-block:: python
804|
805|    @pass_context
806|    def filter(context, value):
807|        result = do_something(value)
808|
809|        if context.eval_ctx.autoescape:
810|            result = Markup(result)
811|
812|        return result
813|
814|The evaluation context must not be modified at runtime.  Modifications
815|must only happen with a :class:`nodes.EvalContextModifier` and
816|:class:`nodes.ScopedEvalContextModifier` from an extension, not on the
817|eval context object itself.
818|
819|.. autoclass:: jinja2.nodes.EvalContext
820|
821|   .. attribute:: autoescape
822|
823|      `True` or `False` depending on if autoescaping is active or not.
824|
825|   .. attribute:: volatile
826|
827|      `True` if the compiler cannot evaluate some expressions at compile
828|      time.  At runtime this should always be `False`.
829|
830|
831|.. _global-namespace:
832|
833|The Global Namespace
834|--------------------
835|
836|The global namespace stores variables and functions that should be
837|available without needing to pass them to :meth:`Template.render`. They
838|are also available to templates that are imported or included without
839|context. Most applications should only use :attr:`Environment.globals`.
840|
841|:attr:`Environment.globals` are intended for data that is common to all
842|templates loaded by that environment. :attr:`Template.globals` are
843|intended for data that is common to all renders of that template, and
844|default to :attr:`Environment.globals` unless they're given in
845|:meth:`Environment.get_template`, etc. Data that is specific to a
846|render should be passed as context to :meth:`Template.render`.
847|
848|Only one set of globals is used during any specific rendering. If
849|templates A and B both have template globals, and B extends A, then
850|only B's globals are used for both when using ``b.render()``.
851|
852|Environment globals should not be changed after loading any templates,
853|and template globals should not be changed at any time after loading the
854|template. Changing globals after loading a template will result in
855|unexpected behavior as they may be shared between the environment and
856|other templates.
857|
858|
859|.. _low-level-api:
860|
861|Low Level API
862|-------------
863|
864|The low level API exposes functionality that can be useful to understand some
865|implementation details, debugging purposes or advanced :ref:`extension
866|<jinja-extensions>` techniques.  Unless you know exactly what you are doing we
867|don't recommend using any of those.
868|
869|.. automethod:: Environment.lex
870|
871|.. automethod:: Environment.parse
872|
873|.. automethod:: Environment.preprocess
874|
875|.. automethod:: Template.new_context
876|
877|.. method:: Template.root_render_func(context)
878|
879|    This is the low level render function.  It's passed a :class:`Context`
880|    that has to be created by :meth:`new_context` of the same template or
881|    a compatible template.  This render function is generated by the
882|    compiler from the template code and returns a generator that yields
883|    strings.
884|
885|    If an exception in the template code happens the template engine will
886|    not rewrite the exception but pass through the original one.  As a
887|    matter of fact this function should only be called from within a
888|    :meth:`render` / :meth:`generate` / :meth:`stream` call.
889|
890|.. attribute:: Template.blocks
891|
892|    A dict of block render functions.  Each of these functions works exactly
893|    like the :meth:`root_render_func` with the same limitations.
894|
895|.. attribute:: Template.is_up_to_date
896|
897|    This attribute is `False` if there is a newer version of the template
898|    available, otherwise `True`.
899|
900|.. admonition:: Note
901|
902|    The low-level API is fragile.  Future Jinja versions will try not to
903|    change it in a backwards incompatible way but modifications in the Jinja
904|    core may shine through.  For example if Jinja introduces a new AST node
905|    in later versions that may be returned by :meth:`~Environment.parse`.
906|
907|The Meta API
908|------------
909|
910|.. versionadded:: 2.2
911|
912|The meta API returns some information about abstract syntax trees that
913|could help applications to implement more advanced template concepts.  All
914|the functions of the meta API operate on an abstract syntax tree as
915|returned by the :meth:`Environment.parse` method.
916|
917|.. autofunction:: jinja2.meta.find_undeclared_variables
918|
919|.. autofunction:: jinja2.meta.find_referenced_templates

1|.. _jinja-extensions:
2|
3|Extensions
4|==========
5|
6|Jinja supports extensions that can add extra filters, tests, globals or even
7|extend the parser.  The main motivation of extensions is to move often used
8|code into a reusable class like adding support for internationalization.
9|
10|
11|Adding Extensions
12|-----------------
13|
14|Extensions are added to the Jinja environment at creation time.  To add an
15|extension pass a list of extension classes or import paths to the
16|``extensions`` parameter of the :class:`~jinja2.Environment` constructor.  The following
17|example creates a Jinja environment with the i18n extension loaded::
18|
19|    jinja_env = Environment(extensions=['jinja2.ext.i18n'])
20|
21|To add extensions after creation time, use the :meth:`~jinja2.Environment.add_extension` method::
22|
23|    jinja_env.add_extension('jinja2.ext.debug')
24|
25|
26|.. _i18n-extension:
27|
28|i18n Extension
29|--------------
30|
31|**Import name:** ``jinja2.ext.i18n``
32|
33|The i18n extension can be used in combination with `gettext`_ or
34|`Babel`_.  When it's enabled, Jinja provides a ``trans`` statement that
35|marks a block as translatable and calls ``gettext``.
36|
37|After enabling, an application has to provide functions for ``gettext``,
38|``ngettext``, and optionally ``pgettext`` and ``npgettext``, either
39|globally or when rendering. A ``_()`` function is added as an alias to
40|the ``gettext`` function.
41|
42|A convenient way to provide these functions is to call one of the below
43|methods depending on the translation system in use. If you do not require
44|actual translation, use ``Environment.install_null_translations`` to
45|install no-op functions.
46|
47|Environment Methods
48|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
49|
50|After enabling the extension, the environment provides the following
51|additional methods:
52|
53|.. method:: jinja2.Environment.install_gettext_translations(translations, newstyle=False)
54|
55|    Installs a translation globally for the environment. The
56|    ``translations`` object must implement ``gettext``, ``ngettext``,
57|    and optionally ``pgettext`` and ``npgettext``.
58|    :class:`gettext.NullTranslations`, :class:`gettext.GNUTranslations`,
59|    and `Babel`_\s ``Translations`` are supported.
60|
61|    .. versionchanged:: 3.0
62|        Added ``pgettext`` and ``npgettext``.
63|
64|    .. versionchanged:: 2.5
65|        Added new-style gettext support.
66|
67|.. method:: jinja2.Environment.install_null_translations(newstyle=False)
68|
69|    Install no-op gettext functions. This is useful if you want to
70|    prepare the application for internationalization but don't want to
71|    implement the full system yet.
72|
73|    .. versionchanged:: 2.5 Added new-style gettext support.
74|
75|.. method:: jinja2.Environment.install_gettext_callables(gettext, ngettext, newstyle=False, pgettext=None, npgettext=None)
76|
77|    Install the given ``gettext``, ``ngettext``, ``pgettext``, and
78|    ``npgettext`` callables into the environment. They should behave
79|    exactly like :func:`gettext.gettext`, :func:`gettext.ngettext`,
80|    :func:`gettext.pgettext` and :func:`gettext.npgettext`.
81|
82|    If ``newstyle`` is activated, the callables are wrapped to work like
83|    newstyle callables.  See :ref:`newstyle-gettext` for more information.
84|
85|    .. versionchanged:: 3.0
86|        Added ``pgettext`` and ``npgettext``.
87|
88|    .. versionadded:: 2.5
89|        Added new-style gettext support.
90|
91|.. method:: jinja2.Environment.uninstall_gettext_translations()
92|
93|    Uninstall the environment's globally installed translation.
94|
95|.. method:: jinja2.Environment.extract_translations(source)
96|
97|    Extract localizable strings from the given template node or source.
98|
99|    For every string found this function yields a ``(lineno, function,
100|    message)`` tuple, where:
101|
102|    -   ``lineno`` is the number of the line on which the string was
103|        found.
104|    -   ``function`` is the name of the ``gettext`` function used (if
105|        the string was extracted from embedded Python code).
106|    -   ``message`` is the string itself, or a tuple of strings for
107|        functions with multiple arguments.
108|
109|    If `Babel`_ is installed, see :ref:`babel-integration` to extract
110|    the strings.
111|
112|For a web application that is available in multiple languages but gives
113|all the users the same language (for example, multilingual forum
114|software installed for a French community), the translation may be
115|installed when the environment is created.
116|
117|.. code-block:: python
118|
119|    translations = get_gettext_translations()
120|    env = Environment(extensions=["jinja2.ext.i18n"])
121|    env.install_gettext_translations(translations)
122|
123|The ``get_gettext_translations`` function would return the translator
124|for the current configuration, for example by using ``gettext.find``.
125|
126|The usage of the ``i18n`` extension for template designers is covered in
127|:ref:`the template documentation <i18n-in-templates>`.
128|
129|.. _gettext: https://docs.python.org/3/library/gettext.html
130|.. _Babel: https://babel.pocoo.org/
131|
132|
133|Whitespace Trimming
134|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
135|
136|.. versionadded:: 2.10
137|
138|Within ``{% trans %}`` blocks, it can be useful to trim line breaks and
139|whitespace so that the block of text looks like a simple string with
140|single spaces in the translation file.
141|
142|Linebreaks and surrounding whitespace can be automatically trimmed by
143|enabling the ``ext.i18n.trimmed`` :ref:`policy <ext-i18n-trimmed>`.
144|
145|
146|.. _newstyle-gettext:
147|
148|New Style Gettext
149|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
150|
151|.. versionadded:: 2.5
152|
153|New style gettext calls are less to type, less error prone, and support
154|autoescaping better.
155|
156|You can use "new style" gettext calls by setting
157|``env.newstyle_gettext = True`` or passing ``newstyle=True`` to
158|``env.install_translations``. They are fully supported by the Babel
159|extraction tool, but might not work as expected with other extraction
160|tools.
161|
162|With standard ``gettext`` calls, string formatting is a separate step
163|done with the ``|format`` filter. This requires duplicating work for
164|``ngettext`` calls.
165|
166|.. sourcecode:: jinja
167|
168|    {{ gettext("Hello, World!") }}
169|    {{ gettext("Hello, %(name)s!")|format(name=name) }}
170|    {{ ngettext(
171|           "%(num)d apple", "%(num)d apples", apples|count
172|       )|format(num=apples|count) }}
173|    {{ pgettext("greeting", "Hello, World!") }}
174|    {{ npgettext(
175|           "fruit", "%(num)d apple", "%(num)d apples", apples|count
176|       )|format(num=apples|count) }}
177|
178|New style ``gettext`` make formatting part of the call, and behind the
179|scenes enforce more consistency.
180|
181|.. sourcecode:: jinja
182|
183|    {{ gettext("Hello, World!") }}
184|    {{ gettext("Hello, %(name)s!", name=name) }}
185|    {{ ngettext("%(num)d apple", "%(num)d apples", apples|count) }}
186|    {{ pgettext("greeting", "Hello, World!") }}
187|    {{ npgettext("fruit", "%(num)d apple", "%(num)d apples", apples|count) }}
188|
189|The advantages of newstyle gettext are:
190|
191|-   There's no separate formatting step, you don't have to remember to
192|    use the ``|format`` filter.
193|-   Only named placeholders are allowed. This solves a common problem
194|    translators face because positional placeholders can't switch
195|    positions meaningfully. Named placeholders always carry semantic
196|    information about what value goes where.
197|-   String formatting is used even if no placeholders are used, which
198|    makes all strings use a consistent format. Remember to escape any
199|    raw percent signs as ``%%``, such as ``100%%``.
200|-   The translated string is marked safe, formatting performs escaping
201|    as needed. Mark a parameter as ``|safe`` if it has already been
202|    escaped.
203|
204|
205|Expression Statement
206|--------------------
207|
208|**Import name:** ``jinja2.ext.do``
209|
210|The "do" aka expression-statement extension adds a simple ``do`` tag to the
211|template engine that works like a variable expression but ignores the
212|return value.
213|
214|.. _loopcontrols-extension:
215|
216|Loop Controls
217|-------------
218|
219|**Import name:** ``jinja2.ext.loopcontrols``
220|
221|This extension adds support for ``break`` and ``continue`` in loops.  After
222|enabling, Jinja provides those two keywords which work exactly like in
223|Python.
224|
225|.. _with-extension:
226|
227|With Statement
228|--------------
229|
230|**Import name:** ``jinja2.ext.with_``
231|
232|.. versionchanged:: 2.9
233|
234|    This extension is now built-in and no longer does anything.
235|
236|.. _autoescape-extension:
237|
238|Autoescape Extension
239|--------------------
240|
241|**Import name:** ``jinja2.ext.autoescape``
242|
243|.. versionchanged:: 2.9
244|
245|    This extension was removed and is now built-in. Enabling the
246|    extension no longer does anything.
247|
248|
249|.. _debug-extension:
250|
251|Debug Extension
252|---------------
253|
254|**Import name:** ``jinja2.ext.debug``
255|
256|Adds a ``{% debug %}`` tag to dump the current context as well as the
257|available filters and tests. This is useful to see what's available to
258|use in the template without setting up a debugger.
259|
260|
261|.. _writing-extensions:
262|
263|Writing Extensions
264|------------------
265|
266|.. module:: jinja2.ext
267|
268|By writing extensions you can add custom tags to Jinja.  This is a non-trivial
269|task and usually not needed as the default tags and expressions cover all
270|common use cases.  The i18n extension is a good example of why extensions are
271|useful. Another one would be fragment caching.
272|
273|When writing extensions you have to keep in mind that you are working with the
274|Jinja template compiler which does not validate the node tree you are passing
275|to it.  If the AST is malformed you will get all kinds of compiler or runtime
276|errors that are horrible to debug.  Always make sure you are using the nodes
277|you create correctly.  The API documentation below shows which nodes exist and
278|how to use them.
279|
280|
281|Example Extensions
282|------------------
283|
284|Cache
285|~~~~~
286|
287|The following example implements a ``cache`` tag for Jinja by using the
288|`cachelib`_ library:
289|
290|.. literalinclude:: examples/cache_extension.py
291|    :language: python
292|
293|And here is how you use it in an environment::
294|
295|    from jinja2 import Environment
296|    from cachelib import SimpleCache
297|
298|    env = Environment(extensions=[FragmentCacheExtension])
299|    env.fragment_cache = SimpleCache()
300|
301|Inside the template it's then possible to mark blocks as cacheable.  The
302|following example caches a sidebar for 300 seconds:
303|
304|.. sourcecode:: html+jinja
305|
306|    {% cache 'sidebar', 300 %}
307|    <div class="sidebar">
308|        ...
309|    </div>
310|    {% endcache %}
311|
312|.. _cachelib: https://github.com/pallets/cachelib
313|
314|
315|Inline ``gettext``
316|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
317|
318|The following example demonstrates using :meth:`Extension.filter_stream`
319|to parse calls to the ``_()`` gettext function inline with static data
320|without needing Jinja blocks.
321|
322|.. code-block:: html
323|
324|        <h1>_(Welcome)</h1>
325|        <p>_(This is a paragraph)</p>
326|
327|It requires the i18n extension to be loaded and configured.
328|
329|.. literalinclude:: examples/inline_gettext_extension.py
330|    :language: python
331|
332|
333|Extension API
334|-------------
335|
336|Extension
337|~~~~~~~~~
338|
339|Extensions always have to extend the :class:`jinja2.ext.Extension` class:
340|
341|.. autoclass:: Extension
342|    :members: preprocess, filter_stream, parse, attr, call_method
343|
344|    .. attribute:: identifier
345|
346|        The identifier of the extension.  This is always the true import name
347|        of the extension class and must not be changed.
348|
349|    .. attribute:: tags
350|
351|        If the extension implements custom tags this is a set of tag names
352|        the extension is listening for.
353|
354|
355|Parser
356|~~~~~~
357|
358|The parser passed to :meth:`Extension.parse` provides ways to parse
359|expressions of different types.  The following methods may be used by
360|extensions:
361|
362|.. autoclass:: jinja2.parser.Parser
363|    :members: parse_expression, parse_tuple, parse_assign_target,
364|              parse_statements, free_identifier, fail
365|
366|    .. attribute:: filename
367|
368|        The filename of the template the parser processes.  This is **not**
369|        the load name of the template.  For the load name see :attr:`name`.
370|        For templates that were not loaded form the file system this is
371|        ``None``.
372|
373|    .. attribute:: name
374|
375|        The load name of the template.
376|
377|    .. attribute:: stream
378|
379|        The current :class:`~jinja2.lexer.TokenStream`
380|
381|.. autoclass:: jinja2.lexer.TokenStream
382|   :members: push, look, eos, skip, __next__, next_if, skip_if, expect
383|
384|   .. attribute:: current
385|
386|        The current :class:`~jinja2.lexer.Token`.
387|
388|.. autoclass:: jinja2.lexer.Token
389|    :members: test, test_any
390|
391|    .. attribute:: lineno
392|
393|        The line number of the token
394|
395|    .. attribute:: type
396|
397|        The type of the token.  This string is interned so you may compare
398|        it with arbitrary strings using the ``is`` operator.
399|
400|    .. attribute:: value
401|
402|        The value of the token.
403|
404|There is also a utility function in the lexer module that can count newline
405|characters in strings:
406|
407|.. autofunction:: jinja2.lexer.count_newlines
408|
409|
410|AST
411|~~~
412|
413|The AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) is used to represent a template after parsing.
414|It's build of nodes that the compiler then converts into executable Python
415|code objects.  Extensions that provide custom statements can return nodes to
416|execute custom Python code.
417|
418|The list below describes all nodes that are currently available.  The AST may
419|change between Jinja versions but will stay backwards compatible.
420|
421|For more information have a look at the repr of :meth:`jinja2.Environment.parse`.
422|
423|.. module:: jinja2.nodes
424|
425|.. jinja:nodes:: jinja2.nodes.Node
426|
427|.. autoexception:: Impossible

1|Switching From Other Template Engines
2|=====================================
3|
4|This is a brief guide on some of the differences between Jinja syntax
5|and other template languages. See :doc:`/templates` for a comprehensive
6|guide to Jinja syntax and features.
7|
8|
9|Django
10|------
11|
12|If you have previously worked with Django templates, you should find
13|Jinja very familiar. Many of the syntax elements look and work the same.
14|However, Jinja provides some more syntax elements, and some work a bit
15|differently.
16|
17|This section covers the template changes. The API, including extension
18|support, is fundamentally different so it won't be covered here.
19|
20|Django supports using Jinja as its template engine, see
21|https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/templates/#support-for-template-engines.
22|
23|
24|Method Calls
25|~~~~~~~~~~~~
26|
27|In Django, methods are called implicitly, without parentheses.
28|
29|.. code-block:: django
30|
31|    {% for page in user.get_created_pages %}
32|        ...
33|    {% endfor %}
34|
35|In Jinja, using parentheses is required for calls, like in Python. This
36|allows you to pass variables to the method, which is not possible
37|in Django. This syntax is also used for calling macros.
38|
39|.. code-block:: jinja
40|
41|    {% for page in user.get_created_pages() %}
42|        ...
43|    {% endfor %}
44|
45|
46|Filter Arguments
47|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
48|
49|In Django, one literal value can be passed to a filter after a colon.
50|
51|.. code-block:: django
52|
53|    {{ items|join:", " }}
54|
55|In Jinja, filters can take any number of positional and keyword
56|arguments in parentheses, like function calls. Arguments can also be
57|variables instead of literal values.
58|
59|.. code-block:: jinja
60|
61|    {{ items|join(", ") }}
62|
63|
64|Tests
65|~~~~~
66|
67|In addition to filters, Jinja also has "tests" used with the ``is``
68|operator. This operator is not the same as the Python operator.
69|
70|.. code-block:: jinja
71|
72|    {% if user.user_id is odd %}
73|        {{ user.username|e }} is odd
74|    {% else %}
75|        hmm. {{ user.username|e }} looks pretty normal
76|    {% endif %}
77|
78|Loops
79|~~~~~
80|
81|In Django, the special variable for the loop context is called
82|``forloop``, and the ``empty`` is used for no loop items.
83|
84|.. code-block:: django
85|
86|    {% for item in items %}
87|        {{ forloop.counter }}. {{ item }}
88|    {% empty %}
89|        No items!
90|    {% endfor %}
91|
92|In Jinja, the special variable for the loop context is called ``loop``,
93|and the ``else`` block is used for no loop items.
94|
95|.. code-block:: jinja
96|
97|    {% for item in items %}
98|        {{ loop.index }}. {{ item }}
99|    {% else %}
100|        No items!
101|    {% endfor %}
102|
103|
104|Cycle
105|~~~~~
106|
107|In Django, the ``{% cycle %}`` can be used in a for loop to alternate
108|between values per loop.
109|
110|.. code-block:: django
111|
112|    {% for user in users %}
113|        <li class="{% cycle 'odd' 'even' %}">{{ user }}</li>
114|    {% endfor %}
115|
116|In Jinja, the ``loop`` context has a ``cycle`` method.
117|
118|.. code-block:: jinja
119|
120|    {% for user in users %}
121|        <li class="{{ loop.cycle('odd', 'even') }}">{{ user }}</li>
122|    {% endfor %}
123|
124|A cycler can also be assigned to a variable and used outside or across
125|loops with the ``cycle()`` global function.
126|
127|
128|Mako
129|----
130|
131|You can configure Jinja to look more like Mako:
132|
133|.. code-block:: python
134|
135|    env = Environment(
136|        block_start_string="<%",
137|        block_end_string="%>",
138|        variable_start_string="${",
139|        variable_end_string="}",
140|        comment_start_string="<%doc>",
141|        commend_end_string="</%doc>",
142|        line_statement_prefix="%",
143|        line_comment_prefix="##",
144|    )
145|
146|With an environment configured like that, Jinja should be able to
147|interpret a small subset of Mako templates without any changes.
148|
149|Jinja does not support embedded Python code, so you would have to move
150|that out of the template. You could either process the data with the
151|same code before rendering, or add a global function or filter to the
152|Jinja environment.
153|
154|The syntax for defs (which are called macros in Jinja) and template
155|inheritance is different too.
156|
157|The following Mako template:
158|
159|.. code-block:: mako
160|
161|    <%inherit file="layout.html" />
162|    <%def name="title()">Page Title</%def>
163|    <ul>
164|    % for item in list:
165|        <li>${item}</li>
166|    % endfor
167|    </ul>
168|
169|Looks like this in Jinja with the above configuration:
170|
171|.. code-block:: jinja
172|
173|    <% extends "layout.html" %>
174|    <% block title %>Page Title<% endblock %>
175|    <% block body %>
176|    <ul>
177|    % for item in list:
178|        <li>${item}</li>
179|    % endfor
180|    </ul>
181|    <% endblock %>

--- FILE: docs/sandbox.rst ---
1|Sandbox
2|=======
3|
4|The Jinja sandbox can be used to render untrusted templates. Access to
5|attributes, method calls, operators, mutating data structures, and
6|string formatting can be intercepted and prohibited.
7|
8|.. code-block:: pycon
9|
10|    >>> from jinja2.sandbox import SandboxedEnvironment
11|    >>> env = SandboxedEnvironment()
12|    >>> func = lambda: "Hello, Sandbox!"
13|    >>> env.from_string("{{ func() }}").render(func=func)
14|    'Hello, Sandbox!'
15|    >>> env.from_string("{{ func.__code__.co_code }}").render(func=func)
16|    Traceback (most recent call last):
17|      ...
18|    SecurityError: access to attribute '__code__' of 'function' object is unsafe.
19|
20|A sandboxed environment can be useful, for example, to allow users of an
21|internal reporting system to create custom emails. You would document
22|what data is available in the templates, then the user would write a
23|template using that information. Your code would generate the report
24|data and pass it to the user's sandboxed template to render.
25|
26|
27|Security Considerations
28|-----------------------
29|
30|The sandbox alone is not a solution for perfect security. Keep these
31|things in mind when using the sandbox.
32|
33|Templates can still raise errors when compiled or rendered. Your code
34|should attempt to catch errors instead of crashing.
35|
36|It is possible to construct a relatively small template that renders to
37|a very large amount of output, which could correspond to a high use of
38|CPU or memory. You should run your application with limits on resources
39|such as CPU and memory to mitigate this.
40|
41|Jinja only renders text, it does not understand, for example, JavaScript
42|code. Depending on how the rendered template will be used, you may need
43|to do other postprocessing to restrict the output.
44|
45|Pass only the data that is relevant to the template. Avoid passing
46|global data, or objects with methods that have side effects. By default
47|the sandbox prevents private and internal attribute access. You can
48|override :meth:`~SandboxedEnvironment.is_safe_attribute` to further
49|restrict attributes access. Decorate methods with :func:`unsafe` to
50|prevent calling them from templates when passing objects as data. Use
51|:class:`ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment` to prevent modifying lists and
52|dictionaries.
53|
54|
55|API
56|---
57|
58|.. module:: jinja2.sandbox
59|
60|.. autoclass:: SandboxedEnvironment([options])
61|    :members: is_safe_attribute, is_safe_callable, default_binop_table,
62|              default_unop_table, intercepted_binops, intercepted_unops,
63|              call_binop, call_unop
64|
65|.. autoclass:: ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment([options])
66|
67|.. autoexception:: SecurityError
68|
69|.. autofunction:: unsafe
70|
71|.. autofunction:: is_internal_attribute
72|
73|.. autofunction:: modifies_known_mutable
74|
75|
76|Operator Intercepting
77|---------------------
78|
79|For performance, Jinja outputs operators directly when compiling. This
80|means it's not possible to intercept operator behavior by overriding
81|:meth:`SandboxEnvironment.call <Environment.call>` by default, because
82|operator special methods are handled by the Python interpreter, and
83|might not correspond with exactly one method depending on the operator's
84|use.
85|
86|The sandbox can instruct the compiler to output a function to intercept
87|certain operators instead. Override
88|:attr:`SandboxedEnvironment.intercepted_binops` and
89|:attr:`SandboxedEnvironment.intercepted_unops` with the operator symbols
90|you want to intercept. The compiler will replace the symbols with calls
91|to :meth:`SandboxedEnvironment.call_binop` and
92|:meth:`SandboxedEnvironment.call_unop` instead. The default
93|implementation of those methods will use
94|:attr:`SandboxedEnvironment.binop_table` and
95|:attr:`SandboxedEnvironment.unop_table` to translate operator symbols
96|into :mod:`operator` functions.
97|
98|For example, the power (``**``) operator can be disabled:
99|
100|.. code-block:: python
101|
102|    from jinja2.sandbox import SandboxedEnvironment
103|
104|    class MyEnvironment(SandboxedEnvironment):
105|        intercepted_binops = frozenset(["**"])
106|
107|        def call_binop(self, context, operator, left, right):
108|            if operator == "**":
109|                return self.undefined("The power (**) operator is unavailable.")
110|
111|            return super().call_binop(self, context, operator, left, right)

--- FILE: docs/faq.rst ---
1|Frequently Asked Questions
2|==========================
3|
4|
5|Why is it called Jinja?
6|-----------------------
7|
8|"Jinja" is a Japanese `Shinto shrine`_, or temple, and temple and
9|template share a similar English pronunciation. It is not named after
10|the `city in Uganda`_.
11|
12|.. _Shinto shrine: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinto_shrine
13|.. _city in Uganda: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinja%2C_Uganda
14|
15|
16|How fast is Jinja?
17|------------------
18|
19|Jinja is relatively fast among template engines because it compiles and
20|caches template code to Python code, so that the template does not need
21|to be parsed and interpreted each time. Rendering a template becomes as
22|close to executing a Python function as possible.
23|
24|Jinja also makes extensive use of caching. Templates are cached by name
25|after loading, so future uses of the template avoid loading. The
26|template loading itself uses a bytecode cache to avoid repeated
27|compiling. The caches can be external to persist across restarts.
28|Templates can also be precompiled and loaded as fast Python imports.
29|
30|We dislike benchmarks because they don't reflect real use. Performance
31|depends on many factors. Different engines have different default
32|configurations and tradeoffs that make it unclear how to set up a useful
33|comparison. Often, database access, API calls, and data processing have
34|a much larger effect on performance than the template engine.
35|
36|
37|Isn't it a bad idea to put logic in templates?
38|----------------------------------------------
39|
40|Without a doubt you should try to remove as much logic from templates as
41|possible. With less logic, the template is easier to understand, has
42|fewer potential side effects, and is faster to compile and render. But a
43|template without any logic means processing must be done in code before
44|rendering. A template engine that does that is shipped with Python,
45|called :class:`string.Template`, and while it's definitely fast it's not
46|convenient.
47|
48|Jinja's features such as blocks, statements, filters, and function calls
49|make it much easier to write expressive templates, with very few
50|restrictions. Jinja doesn't allow arbitrary Python code in templates, or
51|every feature available in the Python language. This keeps the engine
52|easier to maintain, and keeps templates more readable.
53|
54|Some amount of logic is required in templates to keep everyone happy.
55|Too much logic in the template can make it complex to reason about and
56|maintain. It's up to you to decide how your application will work and
57|balance how much logic you want to put in the template.
58|
59|
60|Why is HTML escaping not the default?
61|-------------------------------------
62|
63|Jinja provides a feature that can be enabled to escape HTML syntax in
64|rendered templates. However, it is disabled by default.
65|
66|Jinja is a general purpose template engine, it is not only used for HTML
67|documents. You can generate plain text, LaTeX, emails, CSS, JavaScript,
68|configuration files, etc. HTML escaping wouldn't make sense for any of
69|these document types.
70|
71|While automatic escaping means that you are less likely have an XSS
72|problem, it also requires significant extra processing during compiling
73|and rendering, which can reduce performance. Jinja uses `MarkupSafe`_ for
74|escaping, which provides optimized C code for speed, but it still
75|introduces overhead to track escaping across methods and formatting.
76|
77|.. _MarkupSafe: https://markupsafe.palletsprojects.com/
--- END FILE: docs/faq.rst ---
--- FILE: docs/tricks.rst ---
1|Tips and Tricks
2|===============
3|
4|.. highlight:: html+jinja
5|
6|This part of the documentation shows some tips and tricks for Jinja
7|templates.
8|
9|
10|.. _null-default-fallback:
11|
12|Null-Default Fallback
13|---------------------
14|
15|Jinja supports dynamic inheritance and does not distinguish between parent
16|and child template as long as no `extends` tag is visited.  While this leads
17|to the surprising behavior that everything before the first `extends` tag
18|including whitespace is printed out instead of being ignored, it can be used
19|for a neat trick.
20|
21|Usually child templates extend from one template that adds a basic HTML
22|skeleton.  However it's possible to put the `extends` tag into an `if` tag to
23|only extend from the layout template if the `standalone` variable evaluates
24|to false, which it does by default if it's not defined.  Additionally a very
25|basic skeleton is added to the file so that if it's indeed rendered with
26|`standalone` set to `True` a very basic HTML skeleton is added::
27|
28|    {% if not standalone %}{% extends 'default.html' %}{% endif -%}
29|    <!DOCTYPE html>
30|    <title>{% block title %}The Page Title{% endblock %}</title>
31|    <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" type="text/css">
32|    {% block body %}
33|      <p>This is the page body.</p>
34|    {% endblock %}
35|
36|
37|Alternating Rows
38|----------------
39|
40|If you want to have different styles for each row of a table or
41|list you can use the `cycle` method on the `loop` object::
42|
43|    <ul>
44|    {% for row in rows %}
45|      <li class="{{ loop.cycle('odd', 'even') }}">{{ row }}</li>
46|    {% endfor %}
47|    </ul>
48|
49|`cycle` can take an unlimited number of strings.  Each time this
50|tag is encountered the next item from the list is rendered.
51|
52|
53|Highlighting Active Menu Items
54|------------------------------
55|
56|Often you want to have a navigation bar with an active navigation
57|item.  This is really simple to achieve.  Because assignments outside
58|of `block`\s in child templates are global and executed before the layout
59|template is evaluated it's possible to define the active menu item in the
60|child template::
61|
62|    {% extends "layout.html" %}
63|    {% set active_page = "index" %}
64|
65|The layout template can then access `active_page`.  Additionally it makes
66|sense to define a default for that variable::
67|
68|    {% set navigation_bar = [
69|        ('/', 'index', 'Index'),
70|        ('/downloads/', 'downloads', 'Downloads'),
71|        ('/about/', 'about', 'About')
72|    ] -%}
73|    {% set active_page = active_page|default('index') -%}
74|    ...
75|    <ul id="navigation">
76|    {% for href, id, caption in navigation_bar %}
77|      <li{% if id == active_page %} class="active"{% endif %}>
78|      <a href="{{ href|e }}">{{ caption|e }}</a></li>
79|    {% endfor %}
80|    </ul>
81|    ...
82|
83|.. _accessing-the-parent-loop:
84|
85|Accessing the parent Loop
86|-------------------------
87|
88|The special `loop` variable always points to the innermost loop.  If it's
89|desired to have access to an outer loop it's possible to alias it::
90|
91|    <table>
92|    {% for row in table %}
93|      <tr>
94|      {% set rowloop = loop %}
95|      {% for cell in row %}
96|        <td id="cell-{{ rowloop.index }}-{{ loop.index }}">{{ cell }}</td>
97|      {% endfor %}
98|      </tr>
99|    {% endfor %}
100|    </table>

--- FILE: docs/integration.rst ---
1|Integration
2|===========
3|
4|
5|Flask
6|-----
7|
8|The `Flask`_ web application framework, also maintained by Pallets, uses
9|Jinja templates by default. Flask sets up a Jinja environment and
10|template loader for you, and provides functions to easily render
11|templates from view functions.
12|
13|.. _Flask: https://flask.palletsprojects.com
14|
15|
16|Django
17|------
18|
19|Django supports using Jinja as its template engine, see
20|https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/templates/#support-for-template-engines.
21|
22|
23|.. _babel-integration:
24|
25|Babel
26|-----
27|
28|Jinja provides support for extracting gettext messages from templates
29|via a `Babel`_ extractor entry point called
30|``jinja2.ext.babel_extract``. The support is implemented as part of the
31|:ref:`i18n-extension` extension.
32|
33|Gettext messages are extracted from both ``trans`` tags and code
34|expressions.
35|
36|To extract gettext messages from templates, the project needs a Jinja
37|section in its Babel extraction method `mapping file`_:
38|
39|.. sourcecode:: ini
40|
41|    [jinja2: **/templates/**.html]
42|    encoding = utf-8
43|
44|The syntax related options of the :class:`Environment` are also
45|available as configuration values in the mapping file. For example, to
46|tell the extractor that templates use ``%`` as
47|``line_statement_prefix`` you can use this code:
48|
49|.. sourcecode:: ini
50|
51|    [jinja2: **/templates/**.html]
52|    encoding = utf-8
53|    line_statement_prefix = %
54|
55|:ref:`jinja-extensions` may also be defined by passing a comma separated
56|list of import paths as the ``extensions`` value. The i18n extension is
57|added automatically.
58|
59|Template syntax errors are ignored by default. The assumption is that
60|tests will catch syntax errors in templates. If you don't want to ignore
61|errors, add ``silent = false`` to the settings.
62|
63|.. _Babel: https://babel.readthedocs.io/
64|.. _mapping file: https://babel.readthedocs.io/en/latest/messages.html#extraction-method-mapping-and-configuration
65|
66|
67|Pylons
68|------
69|
70|It's easy to integrate Jinja into a `Pylons`_ application.
71|
72|The template engine is configured in ``config/environment.py``. The
73|configuration for Jinja looks something like this:
74|
75|.. code-block:: python
76|
77|    from jinja2 import Environment, PackageLoader
78|    config['pylons.app_globals'].jinja_env = Environment(
79|        loader=PackageLoader('yourapplication', 'templates')
80|    )
81|
82|After that you can render Jinja templates by using the ``render_jinja``
83|function from the ``pylons.templating`` module.
84|
85|Additionally it's a good idea to set the Pylons ``c`` object to strict
86|mode. By default attribute access on missing attributes on the ``c``
87|object returns an empty string and not an undefined object. To change
88|this add this to ``config/environment.py``:
89|
90|.. code-block:: python
91|
92|    config['pylons.strict_c'] = True
93|
94|.. _Pylons: https://pylonsproject.org/
--- END FILE: docs/integration.rst ---

--- FILE: docs/intro.rst ---
1|Introduction
2|============
3|
4|Jinja is a fast, expressive, extensible templating engine. Special
5|placeholders in the template allow writing code similar to Python
6|syntax. Then the template is passed data to render the final document.
7|
8|It includes:
9|
10|-   Template inheritance and inclusion.
11|-   Define and import macros within templates.
12|-   HTML templates can use autoescaping to prevent XSS from untrusted
13|    user input.
14|-   A sandboxed environment can safely render untrusted templates.
15|-   Async support for generating templates that automatically handle
16|    sync and async functions without extra syntax.
17|-   I18N support with Babel.
18|-   Templates are compiled to optimized Python code just-in-time and
19|    cached, or can be compiled ahead-of-time.
20|-   Exceptions point to the correct line in templates to make debugging
21|    easier.
22|-   Extensible filters, tests, functions, and even syntax.
23|
24|Jinja's philosophy is that while application logic belongs in Python if
25|possible, it shouldn't make the template designer's job difficult by
26|restricting functionality too much.
27|
28|
29|Installation
30|------------
31|
32|We recommend using the latest version of Python. Jinja supports Python
33|3.10 and newer. We also recommend using a `virtual environment`_ in order
34|to isolate your project dependencies from other projects and the system.
35|
36|.. _virtual environment: https://packaging.python.org/tutorials/installing-packages/#creating-virtual-environments
37|
38|Install the most recent Jinja version using pip:
39|
40|.. code-block:: text
41|
42|    $ pip install Jinja2
43|
44|
45|Dependencies
46|~~~~~~~~~~~~
47|
48|These will be installed automatically when installing Jinja.
49|
50|-   `MarkupSafe`_ escapes untrusted input when rendering templates to
51|    avoid injection attacks.
52|
53|.. _MarkupSafe: https://markupsafe.palletsprojects.com/
54|
55|
56|Optional Dependencies
57|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
58|
59|These distributions will not be installed automatically.
60|
61|-   `Babel`_ provides translation support in templates.
62|
63|.. _Babel: https://babel.pocoo.org/
--- END FILE: docs/intro.rst ---
--- FILE: README.md ---
1|<div align="center"><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pallets/jinja/refs/heads/stable/docs/_static/jinja-name.svg" alt="" height="150"></div>
2|
3|# Jinja
4|
5|Jinja is a fast, expressive, extensible templating engine. Special
6|placeholders in the template allow writing code similar to Python
7|syntax. Then the template is passed data to render the final document.
8|
9|It includes:
10|
11|-   Template inheritance and inclusion.
12|-   Define and import macros within templates.
13|-   HTML templates can use autoescaping to prevent XSS from untrusted
14|    user input.
15|-   A sandboxed environment can safely render untrusted templates.
16|-   AsyncIO support for generating templates and calling async
17|    functions.
18|-   I18N support with Babel.
19|-   Templates are compiled to optimized Python code just-in-time and
20|    cached, or can be compiled ahead-of-time.
21|-   Exceptions point to the correct line in templates to make debugging
22|    easier.
23|-   Extensible filters, tests, functions, and even syntax.
24|
25|Jinja's philosophy is that while application logic belongs in Python if
26|possible, it shouldn't make the template designer's job difficult by
27|restricting functionality too much.
28|
29|
30|## In A Nutshell
31|
32|```jinja
33|{% extends "base.html" %}
34|{% block title %}Members{% endblock %}
35|{% block content %}
36|  <ul>
37|  {% for user in users %}
38|    <li><a href="{{ user.url }}">{{ user.username }}</a></li>
39|  {% endfor %}
40|  </ul>
41|{% endblock %}
42|```

--- FILE: docs/nativetypes.rst ---
1|.. module:: jinja2.nativetypes
2|
3|.. _nativetypes:
4|
5|Native Python Types
6|===================
7|
8|The default :class:`~jinja2.Environment` renders templates to strings. With
9|:class:`NativeEnvironment`, rendering a template produces a native Python type.
10|This is useful if you are using Jinja outside the context of creating text
11|files. For example, your code may have an intermediate step where users may use
12|templates to define values that will then be passed to a traditional string
13|environment.
14|
15|Examples
16|--------
17|
18|Adding two values results in an integer, not a string with a number:
19|
20|>>> env = NativeEnvironment()
21|>>> t = env.from_string('{{ x + y }}')
22|>>> result = t.render(x=4, y=2)
23|>>> print(result)
24|6
25|>>> print(type(result))
26|int
27|
28|Rendering list syntax produces a list:
29|
30|>>> t = env.from_string('[{% for item in data %}{{ item + 1 }},{% endfor %}]')
31|>>> result = t.render(data=range(5))
32|>>> print(result)
33|[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
34|>>> print(type(result))
35|list
36|
37|Rendering something that doesn't look like a Python literal produces a string:
38|
39|>>> t = env.from_string('{{ x }} * {{ y }}')
40|>>> result = t.render(x=4, y=2)
41|>>> print(result)
42|4 * 2
43|>>> print(type(result))
44|str
45|
46|Rendering a Python object produces that object as long as it is the only node:
47|
48|>>> class Foo:
49|...     def __init__(self, value):
50|...         self.value = value
51|...
52|>>> result = env.from_string('{{ x }}').render(x=Foo(15))
53|>>> print(type(result).__name__)
54|Foo
55|>>> print(result.value)
56|15
57|
58|Sandboxed Native Environment
59|----------------------------
60|
61|You can combine :class:`.SandboxedEnvironment` and :class:`NativeEnvironment` to
62|get both behaviors.
63|
64|.. code-block:: python
65|
66|    class SandboxedNativeEnvironment(SandboxedEnvironment, NativeEnvironment):
67|        pass
68|
69|API
70|---
71|
72|.. autoclass:: NativeEnvironment([options])
73|
74|.. autoclass:: NativeTemplate([options])
75|    :members: render

188|class StreamFilterExtension(Extension):
189|    def filter_stream(self, stream):
190|        for token in stream:
191|            if token.type == "data":
192|                yield from self.interpolate(token)
193|            else:
194|                yield token
195|
196|    def interpolate(self, token):
197|        pos = 0
198|        end = len(token.value)
199|        lineno = token.lineno
200|        while True:
201|            match = _gettext_re.search(token.value, pos)
202|            if match is None:
203|                break
204|            value = token.value[pos : match.start()]
205|            if value:
206|                yield Token(lineno, "data", value)
207|            lineno += count_newlines(token.value)
208|            yield Token(lineno, "variable_begin", None)
209|            yield Token(lineno, "name", "gettext")
210|            yield Token(lineno, "lparen", None)
211|            yield Token(lineno, "string", match.group(1))
212|            yield Token(lineno, "rparen", None)
213|            yield Token(lineno, "variable_end", None)
214|            pos = match.end()
215|        if pos < end:
216|            yield Token(lineno, "data", token.value[pos:])

1|import re
2|
3|from jinja2.exceptions import TemplateSyntaxError
4|from jinja2.ext import Extension
5|from jinja2.lexer import count_newlines
6|from jinja2.lexer import Token
7|
8|_outside_re = re.compile(r"\\?(gettext|_)\(")
9|_inside_re = re.compile(r"\\?[()]")
10|
11|
12|class InlineGettext(Extension):
13|    """This extension implements support for inline gettext blocks::
14|
15|        <h1>_(Welcome)</h1>
16|        <p>_(This is a paragraph)</p>
17|
18|    Requires the i18n extension to be loaded and configured.
19|    """
20|
21|    def filter_stream(self, stream):
22|        paren_stack = 0
23|
24|        for token in stream:
25|            if token.type != "data":
26|                yield token
27|                continue
28|
29|            pos = 0
30|            lineno = token.lineno
31|
32|            while True:
33|                if not paren_stack:
34|                    match = _outside_re.search(token.value, pos)
35|                else:
36|                    match = _inside_re.search(token.value, pos)
37|                if match is None:
38|                    break
39|                new_pos = match.start()
40|                if new_pos > pos:
41|                    preval = token.value[pos:new_pos]
42|                    yield Token(lineno, "data", preval)
43|                    lineno += count_newlines(preval)
44|                gtok = match.group()
45|                if gtok[0] == "\\":
46|                    yield Token(lineno, "data", gtok[1:])
47|                elif not paren_stack:
48|                    yield Token(lineno, "block_begin", None)
49|                    yield Token(lineno, "name", "trans")
50|                    yield Token(lineno, "block_end", None)
51|                    paren_stack = 1
52|                else:
53|                    if gtok == "(" or paren_stack > 1:
54|                        yield Token(lineno, "data", gtok)
55|                    paren_stack += -1 if gtok == ")" else 1
56|                    if not paren_stack:
57|                        yield Token(lineno, "block_begin", None)
58|                        yield Token(lineno, "name", "endtrans")
59|                        yield Token(lineno, "block_end", None)
60|                pos = match.end()
61|
62|            if pos < len(token.value):
63|                yield Token(lineno, "data", token.value[pos:])
64|
65|        if paren_stack:
66|            raise TemplateSyntaxError(
67|                "unclosed gettext expression",
68|                token.lineno,
69|                stream.name,
70|                stream.filename,
71|            )

1|import itertools
2|import os
3|import re
4|import sys
5|
6|
7|def get_characters():
8|    """Find every Unicode character that is valid in a Python `identifier`_ but
9|    is not matched by the regex ``\\w`` group.
10|
11|    ``\\w`` matches some characters that aren't valid in identifiers, but
12|    :meth:`str.isidentifier` will catch that later in lexing.
13|
14|    All start characters are valid continue characters, so we only test for
15|    continue characters.
16|
17|    _identifier: https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#identifiers
18|    """
19|    for cp in range(sys.maxunicode + 1):
20|        s = chr(cp)
21|
22|        if ("a" + s).isidentifier() and not re.match(r"\w", s):
23|            yield s
24|
25|
26|def collapse_ranges(data):
27|    """Given a sorted list of unique characters, generate ranges representing
28|    sequential code points.
29|
30|    Source: https://stackoverflow.com/a/4629241/400617
31|    """
32|    for _, g in itertools.groupby(enumerate(data), lambda x: ord(x[1]) - x[0]):
33|        lb = list(g)
34|        yield lb[0][1], lb[-1][1]
35|
36|
37|def build_pattern(ranges):
38|    """Output the regex pattern for ranges of characters.
39|
40|    One and two character ranges output the individual characters.
41|    """
42|    out = []
43|
44|    for a, b in ranges:
45|        if a == b:  # single char
46|            out.append(a)
47|        elif ord(b) - ord(a) == 1:  # two chars, range is redundant
48|            out.append(a)
49|            out.append(b)
50|        else:
51|            out.append(f"{a}-{b}")
52|
53|    return "".join(out)
54|
55|
56|def main():
57|    """Build the regex pattern and write it to ``jinja2/_identifier.py``."""
58|    pattern = build_pattern(collapse_ranges(get_characters()))
59|    filename = os.path.abspath(
60|        os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "src", "jinja2", "_identifier.py")
61|    )
62|
63|    with open(filename, "w", encoding="utf8") as f:
64|        f.write("# generated by scripts/generate_identifier_pattern.py")
65|        f.write(f"# Python {sys.version_info[0]}.{sys.version_info[1]}\n")
66|        f.write("import re\n\n")
67|        f.write("pattern = re.compile(\n")
68|        f.write(f'    r"[\\w{pattern}]+"  # noqa: B950\n')
69|        f.write(")\n")
70|
71|
72|if __name__ == "__main__":
73|    main()

1|from jinja2 import nodes
2|from jinja2.ext import Extension
3|
4|
5|class FragmentCacheExtension(Extension):
6|    # a set of names that trigger the extension.
7|    tags = {"cache"}
8|
9|    def __init__(self, environment):
10|        super().__init__(environment)
11|
12|        # add the defaults to the environment
13|        environment.extend(fragment_cache_prefix="", fragment_cache=None)
14|
15|    def parse(self, parser):
16|        # the first token is the token that started the tag.  In our case
17|        # we only listen to ``'cache'`` so this will be a name token with
18|        # `cache` as value.  We get the line number so that we can give
19|        # that line number to the nodes we create by hand.
20|        lineno = next(parser.stream).lineno
21|
22|        # now we parse a single expression that is used as cache key.
23|        args = [parser.parse_expression()]
24|
25|        # if there is a comma, the user provided a timeout.  If not use
26|        # None as second parameter.
27|        if parser.stream.skip_if("comma"):
28|            args.append(parser.parse_expression())
29|        else:
30|            args.append(nodes.Const(None))
31|
32|        # now we parse the body of the cache block up to `endcache` and
33|        # drop the needle (which would always be `endcache` in that case)
34|        body = parser.parse_statements(["name:endcache"], drop_needle=True)
35|
36|        # now return a `CallBlock` node that calls our _cache_support
37|        # helper method on this extension.
38|        return nodes.CallBlock(
39|            self.call_method("_cache_support", args), [], [], body
40|        ).set_lineno(lineno)
41|
42|    def _cache_support(self, name, timeout, caller):
43|        """Helper callback."""
44|        key = self.environment.fragment_cache_prefix + name
45|
46|        # try to load the block from the cache
47|        # if there is no fragment in the cache, render it and store
48|        # it in the cache.
49|        rv = self.environment.fragment_cache.get(key)
50|        if rv is not None:
51|            return rv
52|        rv = caller()
53|        self.environment.fragment_cache.add(key, rv, timeout)
54|        return rv
